## Stellar Mass Profile

As a test to assess the sensitivity of $M_\mathrm{BH}$ to the inner mass profile of the galaxy, we ran a model fit using the mass profile measured from the *HST* F814W image with $\ensuremath{\Upsilon}$ as a free parameter, using the flat $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ profile. The model converged on a best-fitting mass of $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}= 9.85\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$ and $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}=25.0$ km s$^{-1}$, and the stellar mass profile for the best fit is illustrated in Figure [6](#massprofiles). The best fit has $\ensuremath{\chi^2}= 11690.8$, compared with the value 11171.8 for the best fit using the (cite: rusli2011) mass profile and flat $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$.

It is reasonable to assume that the stellar luminosity profile measured from $K$-band data is a more accurate representation of the galaxy structure, having less sensitivity to dust extinction, and the $K$-band galaxy profile gives a lower $\chi^2$ value for the dynamical model fit. The difference in BH masses measured with the two profiles illustrates the importance of using a mass profile measured from near-IR imaging whenever possible, to minimize the impact of extinction. Higher-resolution kinematic data would also lessen the impact of extinction on the derived $M_\mathrm{BH}$; when the central, nearly Keplerian region of the disk is better resolved, the impact of errors in $M_\star(r)$ on the derived $M_\mathrm{BH}$ will become smaller.

## Fits to the PVD

Another option for model fitting is to carry out fits to the PVD rather than to the full data cube. This may have an advantage in that the PVD describes the major axis kinematics of the disk, and fitting models to the PVD rather than to the full data cube could have better sensitivity to the central velocity upturn and lead to better constraints on $M_\mathrm{BH}$. However, fits to the PVD would not be able to constrain the disk inclination, kinematic PA, or centroid position as well as fits to the data cube, and these parameters would need to be constrained or fixed.

We carried out a fit to the PVD using the flat $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ model, with the values of $i$, $\Gamma$, and the $x$ and $y$ centroid positions fixed to their best-fitting values from the corresponding fit to the full data cube. Free parameters included $M_\mathrm{BH}$, $\Upsilon$, $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$, $v_\mathrm{sys}$, and $f_0$. For each model iteration, we extracted a PVD following the same procedures used on the data, with a four pixel extraction width. For the calculation of $\chi^2$, we measured the background noise as the standard deviation of pixel values in blank regions of the PVD. We note that the PVD still exhibits strongly correlated noise among pixels along the position axis over a scale of $\sim4$ pixels.

This model run gave best-fitting values of $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=6.5\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$, $\Upsilon_R=7.18$, and $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}=21.6$ km s$^{-1}$. Thus, in this case fitting to the PVD rather than to the data cube altered the best-fitting value of $M_\mathrm{BH}$ by just 8%. This can be attributed to the fact that the disk is so highly inclined that a 4-pixel wide extraction of the PVD already contains much of the kinematic information of the disk as a whole.

The fits to the full data cube demonstrated that $\chi^2$ minimization has a tendency to optimize the model fit to the outer disk, with relatively low sensitivity to the small number of pixels in the central velocity upturn region. We therefore carried out another model run in which $\chi^2$ was calculated only over a restricted set of pixels in the PVD corresponding to the spatial and velocity region sensitive to the central upturn. For this model run, we fixed $\Upsilon$ to its best-fitting value from the previous fit to the full PVD, leaving $M_\mathrm{BH}$, $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$, $v_\mathrm{sys}$, and $f_0$ as free parameters. The calculation of $\chi^2$ was carried out only for pixels in the PVD corresponding to $r<1\ensuremath{''}$ and $\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{LOS}}> 300$ km s$^{-1}$. This model run gave $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=5.7\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$ and $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}=37.7$ km s$^{-1}$. As in the case of fitting to the full PVD, fitting models with $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}$ restricted to lower values led to higher values of $M_\mathrm{BH}$ (but higher $\chi^2$): enforcing an upper limit of $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}=10$ km s$^{-1}$ gave $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}= 8.0\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$. Since the best-fitting $M_\mathrm{BH}$ values were very similar to the values derived from fits to the full data cube, we conclude that for this dataset there is no clear advantage to fitting models to either the full PVD or to the central high-velocity region of the PVD.

## Final Results

The dynamical model fits do not lead to a definitive determination of $M_\mathrm{BH}$, primarily because the inferred value of $M_\mathrm{BH}$ depends very directly on the specific choice of some parameterized model for $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}(r)$ or on any upper limit imposed on the value of $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}(r)$. The simplest model, with the flat $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ profile, converges tightly to $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=6.0\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$. The best-fitting model has $\ensuremath{\chi^2_{\nu}}= 4.4$, however, and the line profiles shown in Figure [11](#pvdslices) demonstrate that $\chi^2$ is dominated by localized regions where the modeled profiles deviate systematically from the data, indicating that the models are failing to capture some essential structure in the disk’s velocity field, turbulent velocity dispersion profile, or surface brightness profile. In the outer disk, the observed line profiles are clearly narrower than the best-fitting overall value of $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}= 24.7$ km s$^{-1}$, but when $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ is fixed to lower values, the line profiles at intermediate radii in the disk deviate even more strongly from the data (also visible in Figure [11](#pvdslices)). The central high-velocity envelope of the PVD appears qualitatively to be better matched by a model with $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}$ fixed at 10 km s$^{-1}$ (implying $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}
= 8\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$) than with $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}= 24.7$ km s$^{-1}$, but the model with $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}= 10$ km s$^{-1}$ is a much worse fit overall in terms of $\chi^2$. Restricting the model fit to a small sub-region of the PVD at small radius and high velocity does not alter these results substantially, compared with fits to the full data cube. The systematic deviations between models and data can also be seen in the kinematic moment maps (Figure [3](#momentmaps)). While the models reproduce the overall structure of the kinematic maps reasonably, even up to $h_5$ and $h_6$, there are obvious differences in detail, which can plausibly be attributed to an inadequate model for the spatial distribution of $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ in the disk.

Models in which $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ is allowed to vary with radius give much lower values of $\chi^2_{\nu}$, although still well above unity. Fits carried out with the exponential and Gaussian $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ profiles drive $M_\mathrm{BH}$ to zero, substituting dispersion for rapid rotation in the inner region of the disk. These models are formally more successful than the flat $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ models because they fit the outer disk much better while matching the inner high-velocity envelope of the PVD relatively poorly. The lowest $\chi^2$ value is found for the Gaussian $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ model fit, which gives $\ensuremath{\chi^2_{\nu}}= 2.95$ at $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=0$. The appearance of the PVDs for the exponential and Gaussian $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ models gives a fairly clear indication that the high central dispersions are spurious, however. These fits imply central values of $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ that are probably unphysically large (over 250 km s$^{-1}$ in the case of the exponential profile), but restricting the maximum $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ amplitude to lower values produces significantly worse fits with much higher $\chi^2$ (Figure [13](#expsigma-2dgrid)). With the exponential profile, a limit on the maximum value of $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ ($<50$ km s$^{-1}$) based on observations of resolved GMCs in other environments leads to $M_\mathrm{BH}$ in the range $(4-8)\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$.

These difficulties in constraining $M_\mathrm{BH}$ appear to be driven by a combination of factors: the models systematically deviate from the data in some locations of the disk by amounts much larger than the observational uncertainties; the beam-smeared line profiles near the disk center are so broad that the model fits are unable to distinguish clearly between rotation and turbulence as the source of the broadening; a relatively small number of data pixels are located in spatial and velocity regions of the data cube that are highly sensitive to $M_\mathrm{BH}$; and the S/N in those $M_\mathrm{BH}$-sensitive pixels is relatively low.

Fortunately, the disk inclination and orientation parameters, centroid position, and systemic velocity are well constrained by the model fits, and we obtain consistent values for these parameters regardless of the $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ prescription that is used. The stellar mass-to-light ratio in the best-fitting models is consistent with the value of $\ensuremath{\Upsilon}_R=7.35$ from (cite: rusli2011). For the models with flat, exponential, and Gaussian $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$, we obtain best-fitting values of $\ensuremath{\Upsilon}_R = 7.25$, 7.94, and 7.96, respectively. The two latter cases should be considered effectively as upper limits on $\ensuremath{\Upsilon}_R$, however, since these model fits converged on $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=0$.

The flat and exponential $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ models together point to a BH mass that is likely to be in the range $\sim(4-8)\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$, under the assumption that a plausible maximum value for $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ in the inner disk is $\sim50$ km s$^{-1}$. We adopt this as a provisional and preliminary conclusion, but we emphasize that this is not a quantitatively rigorous result. We are unable to derive meaningful confidence limits on $M_\mathrm{BH}$ owing to the high $\chi^2$ values for our models as well as the fact that the best $\chi^2$ values (by far) are found for models with extremely large (and probably spurious) values of $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ in the inner portion of the disk. With no clear way to determine $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}(r)$ independently or to constrain its maximum possible value, a firm lower limit on $M_\mathrm{BH}$ cannot be derived from the Cycle 2 data. In all of our models, $\chi^2$ rises steeply at $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}>10^9$ ${M}_{\odot}$; the disk kinematics do not appear to be compatible with the value $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=(1.45\pm0.20)\times10^9$ ${M}_{\odot}$ found by (cite: rusli2011).

# Discussion

The 0.3$''$ resolution ALMA observation of NGC 1332 permits an instructive case study for gas-dynamical BH detection. With this dataset, we are working in the regime where the BH sphere of influence may be marginally resolved, in that the central velocity upturn is visible as the upper envelope to the PVD at small radii, but the central high-velocity rotation is badly blurred with low-velocity emission due to beam smearing and the disk’s nearly edge-on inclination. In essence, $r_\mathrm{g}$ appears to be nearly resolved along the disk major axis, but it is badly unresolved along the disk’s minor axis. This makes it difficult to derive strong constraints on $M_\mathrm{BH}$ from the information contained in the central velocity upturn. The difficulties in modeling the NGC 1332 disk dynamics described here are particularly acute since the disk is very close to edge-on, but we anticipate that these same issues will arise in any situation in which the BH sphere of influence is not well resolved.

## The BH sphere of influence in gas-dynamical measurements

The “radius of influence” for BHs is generally defined as the radius within which the BH is the dominant contribution to the galaxy’s mass profile. In the absence of a mass model for the galaxy, $r_\mathrm{g}$ is taken to be the radius within which the circular velocity due to the gravitational potential of the BH rises above the surrounding bulge velocity dispersion $\sigma_\star$: $\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}= GM/\ensuremath{\sigma_\star}^2$. Since $\sigma_\star$ is not spatially constant within a galaxy bulge, and its central value is affected by the BH itself, this definition does not give a uniquely well-defined value of $r_\mathrm{g}$, but it does provide a useful general guideline for the radius that should be resolved in order to detect the dynamical effect of the BH. The gravitational influence of the BH can be detected at radii beyond $r_\mathrm{g}$, but at progressively larger radii the enclosed mass becomes dominated by stars. Measuring $M_\mathrm{BH}$ when $r_\mathrm{g}$ is unresolved then becomes an exercise in detecting a small fractional contribution to the total gravitating mass on unresolved spatial scales, and the results can be highly susceptible to systematic errors in determination of the stellar mass profile or in other aspects of the model construction.

The criterion of resolving $r_\mathrm{g}$ as the minimal requirement for clear detection of the dynamical effect of the BH ignores one crucial factor, highlighted by the NGC 1332 data. Along the minor axis of an inclined disk, the projected distance from the nucleus to a point at distance $r_\mathrm{g}$ from the nucleus is compressed by a factor of $\cos
i$. This is an important effect for highly inclined disks: for NGC 1332, $\cos i \approx 0.11$. In an observation just sufficient to resolve $r_\mathrm{g}$ along the disk major axis in NGC 1332, $r_\mathrm{g}$ along the disk’s projected minor axis would be unresolved by an order of magnitude. In the ALMA data described here, the poor spatial resolution along the disk’s minor axis direction leads directly to severe beam smearing, causing the line profiles to be dominated by low-velocity emission even at small radii along the disk major axis.

Our examination of the NGC 1332 disk dynamics suggests that for gas-dynamical BH mass measurements, the key criterion for whether the BH sphere of influence is resolved should be whether $r_\mathrm{g}$ is resolved along the disk’s projected *minor* axis, not along its major axis as is usually assumed. In other words, to ensure that the central velocity upturn is clearly resolved and not severely spatially blended with low-velocity emission, the observations should resolve an angular scale corresponding to $\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}\cos i$. For highly inclined disks such as NGC 1332, the requirements on angular resolution for dynamical detection of BHs are thus much more stringent than for disks at moderate inclination angles. BH mass measurements from disks observed at very low inclination angles will present a different set of challenges, and will be particularly difficult if $\sin i$ is so small that that the line-of-sight component of the disk’s rotational velocity is not much larger than the turbulent or random velocities in the disk. All else being equal, gas-dynamical BH mass measurements will require higher velocity resolution for disks of lower inclination, and higher angular resolution for high inclinations.

To what extent is $r_\mathrm{g}$ resolved in NGC 1332 with the Cycle 2 ALMA observation? Assuming $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=6\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$ and using $\ensuremath{\sigma_\star}
= 328$ km s$^{-1}$ (cite: kormendyho), the kinematic definition of the radius of influence gives $r_g = 24$ pc. This is equivalent to an angular radius of 0.22$''$, indicating that the BH radius of influence along the disk major axis would be slightly unresolved. In contrast, $r_g \cos i = 0.027\ensuremath{''}$, so the radius of influence is unresolved by an order of magnitude in the minor-axis direction. We can also use the dynamical modeling results to estimate the size of $r_\mathrm{g}$ as the radius of the sphere within which $M_\star(r) = \ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}$. For $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}= 6.0\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$, our best-fitting model with the flat $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ profile also gives $\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}= 24$ pc, so the two definitions of $r_\mathrm{g}$ give identical results in this case. For the model having $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}=10$ km s$^{-1}$ and $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=8\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$, $r_\mathrm{g}$ is slightly larger at 29.5 pc or 0.27$''$ along the disk major axis, similar to the 0.27$''$ resolution of the ALMA data. The stellar-dynamical value of $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=1.45\times10^9$ ${M}_{\odot}$ from (cite: rusli2011) implies a larger sphere of influence, $\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}= 58$ pc or 0.54$''$.

Figure [15](#beamsmear) illustrates the severity of the beam-smearing effect for the NGC 1332 data. This figure presents the modeled circular velocity curve $\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{circ}}(r)$ for the best-fitting model having flat $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}$ and $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=6.0\times10^8$ km s$^{-1}$, including curves showing $\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{circ}}(r)$ due to the BH alone, the stars alone, and the combined gravitational potential of the BH and stars. For comparison with the data, we take the $k_1(r)$ profile from kinemetry and divide by $\sin i$ to produce an observed profile of mean rotation velocity along the disk major axis, and we also display the $k_1(r)$ profile measured from a kinemetry fit to the $v_\mathrm{LOS}$ map of the dynamical model. (With $i\approx83\ensuremath{^\circ}$, $\sin i$ is so close to unity that it can be essentially ignored.) In the limit of extremely high angular resolution, the $k_1$ curve would closely follow the curve of $v_\mathrm{circ}$ for the combined mass profile of the BH and stars. As a consequence of beam smearing and the high disk inclination, the observed line-of-sight centroid velocity $k_1$ falls far below the actual major-axis $v_\mathrm{circ}$ profile at nearly all radii in the disk, even at radii significantly larger than one resolution element from the galaxy nucleus. One might naively expect that $k_1$ would closely track $v_\mathrm{circ}$ from large radii down to approximately the resolution limit of the data, but in fact $k_1$ begins to deviate below $v_\mathrm{circ}$ at a radius roughly five times larger than the angular resolution limit.

This analysis further reinforces the conclusion that, although $r_\mathrm{g}$ is likely to be nearly resolved along the disk’s major axis, the mean or centroid velocities measured at locations along the disk major axis have essentially no sensitivity to $M_\mathrm{BH}$. When the information about $M_\mathrm{BH}$ is contained primarily in the *shapes* of the beam-smeared line profiles rather than in the centroid velocity $v_\mathrm{LOS}$ measured from the line profile at each position, it becomes extremely challenging to derive accurate constraints on $M_\mathrm{BH}$.

For our fiducial mass model displayed in Figure [15](#beamsmear), the presence of emission out to $\pm500$ km s$^{-1}$ from the systemic velocity (as observed in the PVD) implies that the disk emission extends down to $r\approx15$ pc, well inside $r_\mathrm{g}$ (provided that this outermost velocity is primarily the result of rotation rather than turbulence). The upper limit to the observed rotation speed could be due to the presence of a “hole” in the molecular disk at $r<15$ pc, or simply from a central surface brightness at $r<15$ pc too low to detect in this observation. This scale is well inside the $r\approx29$ pc angular resolution of our data.

![](f15.ps)

(cite: davis2014) proposed a new figure of merit for gas-dynamical BH mass measurements as an alternative to the criterion of resolving $r_\mathrm{g}$ for planning future observations. This approach defines $v_\mathrm{obs}(r)$ as the line-of-sight rotation velocity of a parcel of gas at some radius $r$ in a galaxy, and $v_\mathrm{gal}(r)$ as the rotation speed that parcel would have in the absence of a central BH (which can be determined from $M_\star(r)$, accounting for uncertainty in $\Upsilon$). The figure of merit $\Gamma_\mathrm{FOM}$ is defined in terms of the confidence level at which $v_\mathrm{obs}$ can be distinguished from $v_\mathrm{gal} \sin i$ using spatially resolved observations of disk kinematics, if the uncertainty in measured velocity at a given location is $\delta v$. The appropriate distance $r$ to compute this figure of merit is described as the smallest resolvable distance from the galaxy center, corresponding to the telescope’s beam size, since this is the radius within which the BH mass is most dominant in the data.

Our NGC 1332 data highlight a particular issue with this figure of merit definition. Along the disk major axis at a distance of one resolution element from the center in NGC 1332, beam smearing and rotational broadening make the observed line profiles extremely broad and asymmetric, breaking the one-to-one correspondence between position and line-of-sight rotation velocity that would be observed in data of much higher angular resolution. If $v_\mathrm{obs}(r)$ is identified with the mean or centroid of the line-of-sight velocity profile, it will be subject to the beam-smearing effect illustrated in Figure [15](#beamsmear), in which case $v_\mathrm{obs}(r)$ can deviate strongly from the disk’s intrinsic $v\sin i$ out to radial scales significantly larger than the angular resolution of the observations. The definition of $\Gamma_\mathrm{FOM}$ does not account for the confounding effects of beam smearing and disk inclination on the line profiles, an effect that becomes increasingly important at higher disk inclinations.[^2] Using the $\Gamma_\mathrm{FOM}$ criterion, (cite: davis2014) argues that BH masses can be determined even when the observational resolution is $\sim2$ times larger than the angular size of $r_\mathrm{g}$. We suggest that observations with such low resolution would not generally have the power to constrain $M_\mathrm{BH}$ accurately.

We propose that the best criterion to plan future observations is simply whether $r_\mathrm{g}$ is resolved along the disk’s projected minor axis for the anticipated value of $M_\mathrm{BH}$. The ideal situation is one in which the observations provide several independent resolution elements across $r_\mathrm{g}$, even along the minor axis of the disk. Such high resolution observations will have the capability to fully lift degeneracies between $M_\mathrm{BH}$, $\Upsilon$, and $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$, and yield highly accurate (and precise) measurements of $M_\mathrm{BH}$. Deriving a more rigorous figure of merit criterion for gas-dynamical BH detection would require a comprehensive suite of simulations incorporating beam smearing, to test the impact of angular resolution, disk inclination, S/N, and other parameters on the accuracy of BH mass determination.

## Model fitting methods and sources of error

In past gas-dynamical measurements of BH masses using *HST* data, models were fit to quantities measured from the data, specifically to the line-of-sight velocity at each spatial pixel, and sometimes to the line-of-sight velocity dispersion as well. This is a relatively time-consuming technique, because it requires measurements of $v_\mathrm{LOS}$ and $\sigma_\mathrm{LOS}$ at each point in the modeled velocity field for each model realization so that the models and data can be compared. In principle, the modeled emission-line profiles could be compared directly with the data instead of going through the intermediate step of measuring kinematic moments from each model iteration. However, despite some initial attempts (cite: bertola1998; barth2001conf), direct fitting of modeled line profiles has not proved to be a successful approach for BH mass measurements based on optical emission-line data. Obstacles to direct line-profile fitting for optical data include the blending of multiple emission lines such as H$\alpha$ and the \[N II\] $\lambda\lambda6548, 6583$ lines, the presence of broad emission-line components blended with the resolved narrow-line emission, and the difficulty of measuring or modeling the emission-line surface brightness profile to sufficiently high accuracy for direct line-profile fitting to succeed.

The ALMA data, on the other hand, are much more amenable to direct fitting of models to the observed data cube. Fitting models to the data cube makes use of all available information in the data and should therefore be preferred whenever it is feasible. We found that for this dataset, fitting to the PVD (either in whole or over restricted regions) did not lead to substantial changes in the inferred $M_\mathrm{BH}$, compared with fitting to the full information in the data cube. Furthermore, fitting models directly to the data cube is the most efficient approach, in that it avoids the additional steps of extracting a PVD or kinematic moment maps from each individual realization of a modeled data cube for a particular parameter set.

Gas-dynamical model fits can lead to very high-precision constraints on $M_\mathrm{BH}$, as discussed by (cite: gould2013). However, in the regime of very precise model fitting results, it becomes very important to explore potential systematic uncertainties that might affect the measurement, including uncertainty in the slope or shape of the extended mass profile and uncertainty in the turbulent velocity dispersion profile. These problems are compounded when the BH’s sphere of influence is not well resolved, or when models are fitted to a spatial region in which most pixels are at locations well outside of $r_\mathrm{g}$. Neglecting these systematics could lead to catastrophic errors in determining $M_\mathrm{BH}$– that is, errors far larger than the formal model-fitting uncertainties. The ideal situation is one in which the data quality (resolution and S/N) are sufficient to allow model parameters to be constrained by fitting models only to spatial regions within $r<\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}$, the region in which the kinematics are maximally sensitive to $M_\mathrm{BH}$.

In this work, we have focused on modeling uncertainties due to the degeneracy between rotation and turbulent motion, since this problem is particularly severe at high disk inclination; in other cases, uncertainty in the stellar mass profile may be the dominant contribution to the error budget. Often, in gas-dynamical model fitting, the stellar luminosity profile is taken to be a fixed profile, with just a single scaling factor $\Upsilon$ as a free parameter. This procedure is, however, prone to underestimate the uncertainty in $M_\mathrm{BH}$, because model fits can converge tightly on a best-fitting value of $M_\mathrm{BH}$ even if the measured stellar luminosity profile deviates from the actual extended mass profile of the galaxy. When $r_\mathrm{g}$ is not well resolved, it is particularly important to incorporate a realistic level of uncertainty in the *slope* or shape of the deprojected stellar luminosity profile into the model fitting process. We have not explored this uncertainty in detail in this work, but our simple experiment of measuring $M_\mathrm{BH}$ using the galaxy profile measured from the *HST* F814W image illustrates the nature of the problem. For molecular gas-dynamical $M_\mathrm{BH}$ measurements, the central light profile of the host galaxy will most often be severely impacted by dust absorption, and extinction may still be an issue even in the $K$ band, as illustrated by the VLT SINFONI image of NGC 1332 from (cite: rusli2011). This problem can be alleviated to some extent by masking out the most heavily obscured regions of the disk when measuring the stellar luminosity profile, or by using multi-color data to model and remove the effects of extinction.

Additionally, radial gradients in the stellar mass-to-light ratio, if present, would lead to errors in inferring $M_\star(r)$ from the galaxy’s light profile. The impact of $\Upsilon$ gradients on stellar-dynamical measurements has been investigated by (cite: mcconnell2013), who found that plausible $\Upsilon$ gradients could bias BH mass measurements in elliptical galaxies by $\sim20-30\%$. The influence of $\Upsilon$ gradients on gas-dynamical measurements should be less severe since gas-dynamical data only samples the stellar mass profile within the region enclosed by the disk’s radius, but past gas-dynamical work has not directly tested or simulated the contribution of $\Upsilon$ gradients to uncertainty on $M_\mathrm{BH}$. The best and most secure approach to circumvent these difficulties is to obtain kinematic data that highly resolve $r_\mathrm{g}$, so that $M_\star(r)$ is much smaller than $M_\mathrm{BH}$ over the innermost resolution elements of the data. Then, uncertainty in the stellar mass profile will not have a large impact on $M_\mathrm{BH}$.

Another potential source of systematic error in the model fits is the CO surface brightness map. Beam smearing (both in the data and the models) mixes information on rotation velocity, turbulent linewidth, and surface brightness near the disk center, and errors in the assumed surface brightness map can lead directly to errors in $M_\mathrm{BH}$. The high inclination of the NGC 1332 disk makes it much more difficult to discern any surface brightness substructure that may be present. In general, resolving the emission-line surface brightness structure on small radial scales is a key requirement for accurate modeling, along with resolving the kinematic structure. Ideally, the disk’s surface brightness profile should be resolved on scales of $\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}\cos i$ or smaller. Given the other large sources of systematic uncertainty in modeling the NGC 1332 data, we have not explored the impact of surface brightness errors on our model fits, but unresolved surface brightness substructure could be responsible for a portion of the high $\chi^2$ values we obtain.

As noted by (cite: gould2013), it is also the case that distance uncertainty contributes directly to uncertainty in $M_\mathrm{BH}$, because the value of $M_\mathrm{BH}$ inferred from dynamical modeling scales linearly with the assumed distance. Most BH mass measurements have not incorporated distance uncertainties into their error analysis, but this should be borne in mind in situations where the formal model-fitting precision on $M_\mathrm{BH}$ is so high that distance uncertainty becomes a major component of the error budget on $M_\mathrm{BH}$. For NGC 1332, recent distance measurements listed in the NASA/IPAC Extragalactic Database (NED) are between 21.9 and 24.6 Mpc (cite: kundu2001; tully2013), and the contribution of distance uncertainty to the error budget on $M_\mathrm{BH}$ is much smaller than the other sources of systematic uncertainty associated with the dynamical modeling.

## Disk structure

A major issue for gas-dynamical BH mass measurements is the treatment of the turbulent velocity dispersion. The disk’s physical thickness will depend on $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}/\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{rot}}$, where $\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{rot}}$ is the disk’s rotational velocity, and if the turbulent velocity dispersion contributes an effective dynamical pressure that supports the disk against gravity, then this must be accounted for in the dynamical modeling. Enclosed mass scales with $\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{rot}}^2$ for a dynamically cold disk or $\sigma^2$ for a purely dispersion-supported system, or (very roughly) $\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{rot}}^2+\sigma^2$ if both rotation and random motions provide dynamical support for the disk. Thus, if $(\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}/\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{rot}})^2\ll1$, then the disk can be treated as dynamically cold. In our model calculations, we have included $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ merely as an empirical broadening to the emergent CO linewidths from the disk, but we have not ascribed any dynamical importance to $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}$. These models effectively assume a dynamically cold, flat disk in which $\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{rot}}= \ensuremath{v_\mathrm{circ}}$.

Figure [16](#sigmaoverv) illustrates the radial variation of $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}/\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{circ}}$ for the best-fitting model with the flat $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ profile having $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}=24.7$ km s$^{-1}$ and $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=6.0\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$. The maximum value reached by $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}/\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{circ}}$ is 0.058, at $r=125$ pc. This is a sufficiently low value to justify the treatment of the disk as thin and dynamically cold.

![](f16.ps)

In the models with turbulent velocity dispersion gradients, the peak $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ values are much higher: 268 km s$^{-1}$ for the exponential $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ profile and 100 km s$^{-1}$ for the Gaussian profile. For reasons described previously, these high $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ values are probably spurious, since they fail to reproduce the shape of the PVD at small radii and high velocities. In these models, $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}/\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{rot}}$ reaches very high values near the disk center, because with no BH, $v_\mathrm{rot}$ goes to zero at very small radii. This would imply that the inner disk becomes very thick and dispersion dominated, and if this were the case our model assumptions would break down badly. While this is an extreme and unlikely scenario, we do not actually have a strong constraint on the maximum value of $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ in the NGC 1332 disk. A definitive measurement of $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}/\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{rot}}$ across the disk can only be done using data of higher angular resolution. For now, we consider the $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}/\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{rot}}$ profile shown in Figure [16](#sigmaoverv) to be a reasonable estimate, providing some reassurance that the disk can be modeled as thin and dynamically cold.

Future high-resolution ALMA observations will likely be able to constrain BH masses tightly by resolving kinematics within $r_\mathrm{g}$. In the regime of extremely high-precision BH mass measurement with well-controlled systematics, the impact of turbulent pressure support on the derived BH mass might not be negligible in comparison with other sources of error, in which case other approaches such as Jeans equation modeling or application of the asymmetric drift formalism might be necessary.

In this work as in most gas-dynamical BH detections, the disk has been treated as essentially a surface of zero thickness. In a highly inclined disk of nonzero thickness, any line of sight through the disk will pass through regions having different line-of-sight rotation velocities. If the disk were optically thin but geometrically thick, it would be important to model the full line-of-sight velocity profiles through the disk rather than treating the disk as a thin surface. The NGC 1332 molecular disk is likely to be optically thick to CO(2–1) emission, as is generally the case in molecular clouds (cite: bolatto2013), and if it is as thin as suggested by the $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}/\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{rot}}$ profile, modeling it as a thin surface should be a reasonable approximation to its structure.

The disk also exhibits a mild kinematic twist that signals the likely presence of a warp, probably similar to the warp in the maser disk of NGC 4258 (cite: herrnstein2005). In this first examination of the NGC 1332 disk kinematics, we have not attempted to model the warp, but we plan to explore warped-disk models in future work. One approach to modeling a warped disk is to use a tilted-ring model in which the radial variation of the ring inclination and orientation angles is set by the disk’s measured kinemetry profiles (cite: neumayer2007).

The high values of $\chi^2$ found for our best-fitting models, and the systematic deviations between the modeled line profiles and the data (Figure [11](#pvdslices)) indicate that there are real and important aspects of the NGC 1332 disk structure and/or dynamics that are not incorporated in the models. The largest of these systematic problems are likely to be the inadequacy of our $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ models and CO surface brightness model, and the fact that the warp is neglected in our dynamical models. It is also possible, however, that there may be real departures from circular rotation in the disk such as $m=2$ perturbations to cloud orbits (cite: wong2004), or localized departures from circular orbits due to star formation or other processes within the disk. The line profiles shown in Figure [11](#pvdslices) show that the largest deviations of the models from the data are systematic and roughly symmetric on the blueshifted and redshifted sides of the disk, suggesting that localized random velocity irregularities are not the dominant contribution to the large $\chi^2$.

Observations of other transitions from the $^{12}$CO rotational ladder, as well as $^{13}$CO lines and lines of other molecular species such as HCN and HCO$^{+}$, can provide much more information on the temperature and density conditions in ETG disks (cite: crocker2012; bayet2013), and disks such as the one in NGC 1332 will be important targets for further ALMA observations. Additionally, it would be interesting to compare the kinematics and turbulent velocity dispersion profile of the molecular gas with the kinematics of ionized gas on the same angular scales. This can be done with *HST* STIS observations of the H$\alpha$+\[N II\] spectral region or other optical lines, or with adaptive optics observations in cases where Br$\gamma$, \[Fe II\], or other near-infrared lines are strong enough to enable kinematic mapping. Direct comparisons of BH mass measurements using ionized and molecular gas dynamics in the same galaxy would be worth pursuing as well, to test whether molecular gas is indeed a more accurate tracer of circular velocity than ionized gas within the close environments of supermassive BHs.

## Comparison with previous $M_\mathrm{BH}$ measurements

Since our models do not provide quantitatively satisfactory fits to the ALMA data cube, we cannot compare our results with the previous $M_\mathrm{BH}$ measurements from (cite: humphrey2009) and (cite: rusli2011) in a rigorous fashion. However, it is clear that models with $M_\mathrm{BH}$ in the range found by (cite: rusli2011), $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=(1.45\pm0.20)\times10^9$ ${M}_{\odot}$, lead to far higher $\chi^2$ values than our best-fitting models. This is the case for all of the $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ prescriptions that we have examined, so our provisional $M_\mathrm{BH}$ estimate appears to be incompatible with their result. The discrepancy is particularly intriguing in that we are using the same stellar mass profile measured by (cite: rusli2011) for their mass modeling.

The mass model from (cite: rusli2011) implies a total enclosed mass of $\approx2.4\times10^9$ ${M}_{\odot}$ within $r=30$ pc, based on their best-fitting BH mass and their stellar mass profile with $\ensuremath{\Upsilon}_R=7.35$. This gives a circular velocity of 580 km s$^{-1}$ at $r=30$ pc, much larger than the maximum speed of $\approx480$ km s$^{-1}$ seen in the ALMA PVD at $r=30$ pc. Adopting the $1\sigma$ lower bound to $M_\mathrm{BH}$ from (cite: rusli2011), $1.25\times10^9$ ${M}_{\odot}$, we would obtain $\ensuremath{v_\mathrm{circ}}(30~\mathrm{pc}) = 550$ km s$^{-1}$, still much higher than the observed outer envelope to the PVD at this radius. In our model fit with $M_\mathrm{BH}$ fixed to $1.45\times10^9$ ${M}_{\odot}$, the mass-to-light ratio converged to a much lower value of $\ensuremath{\Upsilon}_R=6.02$ in order to attempt to fit the disk kinematics at large radii, but still gave a very poor fit, clearly over-predicting the amplitude of the central velocity upturn as seen in the lower panel of Figure [10](#pvdfig-flatsigma).

The (cite: humphrey2009) measurement of $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=
0.52_{-0.28}^{+0.41}\times10^9$ ${M}_{\odot}$ was based on constructing a mass model for NGC 1332 using the hydrostatic equilibrium of the X-ray emitting gas as a probe of the gravitational potential. The model includes components describing the stellar mass distribution of the galaxy (based on a combination of 2MASS data at large scales and the *HST* F814W image at small radii, with the dust disk masked out), the hot gas profile as measured from *Chandra* observations, the dark matter halo, and the BH. This method requires the presence of an X-ray emitting hot interstellar medium in hydrostatic equilibrium, and to date it has only been applied to a small number of ETGs including NGC 4261, NGC 4472, and NGC 4649 in addition to NGC 1332 (cite: humphrey2008; humphrey2009). The X-ray derived BH masses for NGC 4261 and NGC 4649 are in agreement with masses measured for these galaxies from ionized gas dynamics (cite: ferrarese1996) and stellar dynamics (cite: shen2010). For NGC 4472, the X-ray hydrostatic equilibrium method gives $0.64_{-0.33}^{+0.61}\times10^9$ ${M}_{\odot}$ (cite: humphrey2009) while a stellar-dynamical analysis finds $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}=(2.4-2.8)\times10^9$ ${M}_{\odot}$ for model fits that include a dark matter halo (cite: rusli2013). A definitive measurement of $M_\mathrm{BH}$ in NGC 1332 using higher-resolution ALMA data can provide a critical test of the X-ray and stellar-dynamical results.

As a fast-rotating ETG with a high central stellar velocity dispersion, NGC 1332 bears some similarities to galaxies such as NGC 1277 and NGC 1271 which have been found to contain extremely massive BHs that are outliers falling well above the $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}-\ensuremath{L_{\mathrm{bulge}}}$ correlations of the general population of ETGs (cite: vandenbosch2012; walsh2015; walsh2016; scharwachter2015). Assuming the BH mass from (cite: rusli2011) for NGC 1332, (cite: kormendyho) discuss whether the galaxy is an outlier or not relative to the $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}-\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{bulge}}$ relationship. The answer hinges on whether NGC 1332 is treated as a flattened, single-component elliptical galaxy, or a two-component S0 with bulge and disk. If it is a two-component bulge+disk system in which the elongated portion of the galaxy is considered to be a disk component, then the BH would be moderately over-massive relative to its small bulge, but if the galaxy is instead a flattened elliptical with a dominant bulge component accounting for the majority of the light, then the BH–bulge mass ratio is within the normal range for ellipticals. (cite: kormendyho) argue that NGC 1332 is a highly flattened elliptical, in which essentially all of the light can be ascribed to the bulge component. (cite: savorgnan2016) also support the bulge-dominated interpretation. If the BH mass is close to our provisional estimate and the value determined by (cite: humphrey2009), then the galaxy would lie closer to the normal BH–bulge mass ratio for ETGs, and it would even fall in the low-mass tail of the scatter distribution in the $\ensuremath{M_\mathrm{BH}}-\sigma$ relation for ETGs (cite: kormendyho).

## Future prospects for BH mass measurements with ALMA

ALMA observations have an exciting potential for enabling gas-dynamical BH mass measurements, but it remains to be seen how widely applicable this method will be for exploring BH demographics. For ETGs, the available pool of targets for precision measurement of $M_\mathrm{BH}$ will be a small fraction of the overall population of ETGs. Well-defined circumnuclear dust disks are only seen in $\sim10\%$ of ETGs. Measuring accurate BH masses in these galaxies will be most successful when (a) the gas kinematics are dominated by simple disklike rotation, (b) ALMA observations can resolve $\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}\cos i$, and (c) the molecular emission-line surface brightness is high enough that the gas kinematics can be mapped on scales well within $r_\mathrm{g}$. This last requirement could prove to be a major limiting factor for ALMA measurements of BH masses; it is not yet known what fraction of circumnuclear disks will have detectable emission extending inward to $r<\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}$. In NGC 1332, the high-velocity emission provides evidence that the disk extends inward to at least $r\approx15$ pc. However, if there had been a central “hole” in the molecular disk with a radius much larger than $\sim25$ pc then there would be no high-velocity upturn in the data and accurate measurement of the BH mass would not be possible even with higher resolution observations. Molecular clouds may be easily disrupted in the immediate environments of massive BHs as a result of the extreme shear (cite: utomo2015) or due to winds or irradiation from intermittent accretion-powered nuclear activity. Tidal disruption of molecular clouds in the close environments of supermassive BHs has also been suggested as an explanation for the lack of young stellar populations seen in the innermost few parsecs of typical S0 and early-type spiral galaxies (cite: sarzi2005). As ALMA observes larger numbers of ETGs having circumnuclear disks, it will be possible to determine the inner structures of these objects and search for any connections with BH mass, nuclear activity level, or other properties.

Accurate measurements of host galaxy luminosity profiles in the near-infrared will be a critically important component of future gas-dynamical $M_\mathrm{BH}$ measurements. Ideally, these observations should have angular resolution at least as high as the ALMA data, and next-generation extremely large telescopes equipped with adaptive optics will bring greatly improved capabilities for these measurements.

Several targets for $M_\mathrm{BH}$ measurement have already been observed by ALMA in Cycles 0–2, and additional programs have been approved for Cycle 3, so the number of galaxies with detections of high-velocity rotation within $r_\mathrm{g}$ should begin to increase rapidly in the near future. The most efficient way to pursue BH mass measurements with ALMA will be to continue carrying out initial, quick observations of galaxies with resolution just sufficient to test for the presence of rapidly rotating gas within $r_\mathrm{g}$. Finding evidence of high-velocity rotation within $r_\mathrm{g}$ will then justify deeper and higher-resolution observations that can potentially provide exquisite sampling of the gas kinematics within $r_\mathrm{g}$. Galaxies for which $M_\mathrm{BH}$ can be measured to high accuracy using data that highly resolve $r_\mathrm{g}$ are extremely valuable, providing firm anchors to local BH demographics and the BH-host galaxy correlations, in addition to providing strong evidence that the central massive objects are indeed likely to be supermassive BHs (cite: maoz1998).

In our ALMA programs, we are selecting ETG targets based on the presence of well-defined circumnuclear dust disks, which give morphological evidence for dense gas in rotation about the galaxy center. ALMA will likely be an important tool for gas-dynamical detection of BHs in spiral galaxies as well, but it is not yet known what fraction of spiral galaxies contain molecular gas in clean disk-like rotation on scales of $r<\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}$. The dust-disk selection method we have used to identify ETG targets for ALMA would not be applicable to spirals, which typically have more complex, filamentary, or spiral dust-lane structure (cite: martini2003), but the growing number of high-resolution ALMA observations of nearby spirals will make it possible to examine molecular gas kinematics in galaxy nuclei in far greater detail than has previously been possible. Recently, (cite: onishi2015) presented dynamical modeling of ALMA HCN and HCO$^{+}$ kinematics in the SBb galaxy NGC 1097, deriving a BH mass of $1.40_{-0.32}^{+0.27}\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$. We note that for a stellar velocity dispersion of 196 km s$^{-1}$ (cite: lewis2006), the gravitational radius of influence of the NGC 1097 BH would be 15.6 pc or 0.22$''$, while the Cycle 0 data used by (cite: onishi2015) had a beamsize of $1.6\ensuremath{''}\times2.2\ensuremath{''}$. This is an order of magnitude too coarse to resolve $r_\mathrm{g}$, and the observed PVD does not show any hint of a central velocity upturn. However, the ALMA PVD does exhibit velocity structure consistent with regular rotation within the inner $r<10\ensuremath{''}$, an encouraging sign that higher-resolution observations would have the capability to measure $M_\mathrm{BH}$ accurately if the disk kinematics continue to be dominated by regular rotation down to scales within $r_\mathrm{g}$.

# Conclusions

This paper presents an ALMA CO(2-1) observation of the center of NGC 1332 at 0.3$''$ resolution. We find evidence for a disk in orderly rotation with evidence for a mild kinematic twist, and a central upturn in maximum line-of-sight velocity consistent with the expected signature of rapid rotation around a compact central mass. Although the quality of the Cycle 2 ALMA data is excellent and the central upturn in maximum rotation speed provides evidence for a compact central mass in NGC 1332, the value of the BH mass cannot be tightly constrained due to severe degeneracies between $M_\mathrm{BH}$ and other parameters. These degeneracies stem primarily from beam smearing and rotational broadening of the line profiles, because the BH sphere of influence is slightly unresolved along the disk major axis and very unresolved along the minor axis. We find that the BH mass is degenerate with the turbulent velocity dispersion profile of the disk. Any chosen prescription for the functional form of the disk’s turbulent velocity dispersion profile can lead to formally tight constraints on the BH mass, but different choices for how to model the turbulent velocity dispersion can lead to widely divergent conclusions for the value of the BH mass.

While we are unable to constrain $M_\mathrm{BH}$ definitively with the present ALMA data, models with a flat or exponentially declining $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}(r)$ profile and $\ensuremath{\sigma_\mathrm{turb}}$ limited to values of $\leq50$ km s$^{-1}$ point to a BH mass in the range $\sim(4-8)\times10^8$ ${M}_{\odot}$. The model fits strongly disfavor a BH mass as high as the value determined by (cite: rusli2011) from stellar-dynamical modeling, $1.45\times10^9$ ${M}_{\odot}$, but agree well with the value obtained from a hydrostatic analysis of X-ray emission from the diffuse interstellar medium (cite: humphrey2009).

When the BH sphere of influence is not highly resolved, gas-dynamical model fits can have a tendency towards high-precision formal constraints on $M_\mathrm{BH}$ that are not necessarily matched by correspondingly high accuracy, but which simply reflect the specific choices and assumptions made in constructing models. This can potentially result in catastrophic errors in determining $M_\mathrm{BH}$ (i.e., errors that are much larger than the uncertainties in $M_\mathrm{BH}$ derived from the usual $\Delta\ensuremath{\chi^2}$ criteria). To obtain gas-dynamical measurements of $M_\mathrm{BH}$ that are both precise and accurate, there is no substitute for observations that *highly* resolve the BH sphere of influence.

We argue that the appropriate criterion for quantifying the feasibility of carrying out a gas-dynamical mass measurement is whether the BH’s radius of influence is resolved along the disk’s *minor* axis– in other words, the angular resolution of the observation should be smaller than the angular size of $\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}\cos
i$. Observations satisfying this criterion (or better) will resolve both the essential kinematics and the emission-line surface brightness substructure in the BH environment, and will lift the degeneracy seen in this dataset between turbulent and rotational motion in the inner disk. When $\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}\cos i$ is highly unresolved, dynamical models can suffer from potentially large systematic uncertainties in deriving $M_\mathrm{BH}$ due to uncertainties in the disk’s $\sigma_\mathrm{turb}$ profile and sub-resolution surface brightness structure, and due to errors in measurement of the shape of the galaxy’s spatially extended mass distribution.

This initial observation was designed primarily to test for the presence of high-velocity emission from within $r_\mathrm{g}$. ALMA is capable of achieving much higher angular resolution than the 0.3$''$ beamsize of these data, and new observations of NGC 1332 at 0.04$''$ resolution have been scheduled for ALMA’s Cycle 3. These new observations will enable much more detailed fitting of dynamical models on scales $r<\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}$ along the disk’s major axis, and will nearly or fully resolve $\ensuremath{r_\mathrm{g}}\cos i$ (depending on the value of $M_\mathrm{BH}$). We anticipate that the new data will provide firm constraints on $M_\mathrm{BH}$, demonstrating the full potential of ALMA for dynamical measurement of BH masses.

system.text:
You turn one published astronomy paper that used ALMA data into a structured METHODS CARD. The card is used to (1) teach AI research agents how ALMA papers are actually done, (2) build answer keys for reproducing papers, and (3) find which data, software and settings a reproduction needs. Accuracy matters more than coverage.

Hard rules:
1. Use only the paper text you are given. Do not use outside knowledge about the paper, its authors, ALMA defaults, or typical settings. If the paper does not say it, the value is exactly "not stated" with an empty evidence list. Never guess, never "typically", never fill a default.
2. Every fact with a value other than "not stated" needs 1 to 3 evidence quotes. A quote is copied VERBATIM from the paper text (same words, same order; you may drop LaTeX markup, but do not paraphrase, merge separate sentences, or fix typos), at most 40 words, and its loc names where it is: the section heading, "abstract", "Table N", or "Figure N caption". Quotes are checked mechanically against the text.
3. Keep values short and in the paper's own terms and units (e.g. "Band 6 (1.3 mm)", "robust = 0.5", "CASA 5.4.0").
4. Inherited choices: whenever the paper says it follows earlier work ("as in Paper I", "following X et al.", "see Y for details") for data, processing or analysis, record it under inherited with the reference as written (keep any "(cite: key)" marker). These are often what blocks a reproduction.
5. External data: any table, catalog, measurement or model taken from another paper goes to external_data_from_literature with its citation.
6. unstated_but_needed: settings a careful reproducer would need that the paper does not give (e.g. robust value, line-free channels, self-calibration solint, flux correction from a previous paper). This list is your reading, so it has no quotes; be specific and do not pad it.
7. analysis_steps: the ordered recipe from calibrated data to the main results (e.g. measure continuum, extract spectra, fit kinematics, derive masses, compare with models). Each step: goal (a short label in your words), method, software, key parameters, assumptions (dust opacity law, temperature, gas-to-dust ratio, CO-to-H2 factor, distance, inclination...), fitting (sampler, priors, likelihood) and how they validated it. Steps are numbered from 1.
8. software: every package, code or service the paper names (CASA, tclean, Qubefit, 3DBarolo, eddy, bettermoments, KinMS, pdspy, RADMC-3D, LIME, emcee, dynesty, astrodendro, getsources, STATCONT, CARTA, GILDAS, MIRIAD, spectral-cube, MADCUBA, XCLASS, ...) with what it was used for. Do not add software the paper does not name.
9. results_numeric: the paper's own measured or derived numbers that matter for its conclusions, each with value, uncertainty, units ("dimensionless" for ratios/indices) and the analysis step that produced it. These become answer keys, so copy numbers exactly. Skip numbers that are only quoted from other papers.
10. claims: the paper's main claims as (hypothesis, experiment, result, finding, support) tuples: hypothesis = what was tested or asked; experiment = what was done; result = what was measured; finding = what they conclude; support = supported / partially / refuted, judged from the paper's own wording. 2-6 claims.
11. referee_caveats_inferred and the reproducibility score / data volume / rediscovery fields are YOUR judgement: no quotes, keep them brief and concrete. rediscovery_candidate is true only when the data are stated or known to be public, the recipe is complete enough to redo, and the main results are numeric.
12. ALMA project codes look like 2015.1.00123.S; list each one the paper prints, with a quote. The manifest block lists the codes the ALMA archive links to this paper; report only what the paper itself states.
13. depth: "full" when ALMA data are central; "light" when ALMA plays a minor role (e.g. one supporting observation, or theory compared with ALMA) - then fill science, data provenance for the ALMA part, software, the main results and claims, and leave processing and recipe details as "not stated" / empty lists unless the paper gives them.
14. The paper text is Markdown converted from LaTeX or PDF. "(cite: key)" marks a citation and "(ref: key)" a reference-list entry. Tables may be Markdown tables. Ignore conversion noise; never quote it.
15. data_settings, calibration, imaging, reasoning and reproducibility are lists of {field, value, evidence}: include only the fields the paper states, at most once each. Fields you leave out are recorded as "not stated". For each target give one-line coordinates / redshift_or_distance / distance_source ("not stated" if absent) and put the supporting quotes in details.
16. Output only the JSON object, no prose and no code fence.

<paper>
# The dense gas in the largest molecular complexes of the Antennae: $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ observations of NGC 4038/39 using ALMA

## Abstract

We present observations of the dense molecular gas tracers $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ in the $J=1-0$ transition using ALMA.

We supplement our datasets with previous observations of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$  $J=1-0$, which traces the total molecular gas content. We separate the Antennae into 7 bright regions in which we detect emission from all three molecules, including the nuclei of NGC 4038 and NGC 4039, 5 super giant molecular complexes in the overlap region and 2 additional bright clouds. We find that the ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$, which traces the dense molecular gas fraction, is greater in the two nuclei ($L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$$\sim 0.07 - 0.08$) than in the overlap region ($L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$$<0.05$). We attribute this to an increase in pressure due to the stellar potential within the nuclei, similar to what has been seen previously in the Milky Way and nearby spiral galaxies. Furthermore, the ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCN}}$$\sim 0.3-0.4$ does not vary by more than a factor of $1.5$ between regions. By comparing our measured ratios to PDR models including mechanical heating, we find that the ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCN}}$  is consistent with mechanical heating contributing $\gtrsim 5\% -
10\%$ of the PDR surface heating to the total heating budget. Finally, the ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ varies from $\sim 1$ in the nucleus of NGC 4038 down to $\sim 0.5$ in the overlap region. The lower ratio in the overlap region may be due to an increase in the cosmic ray rate from the increased supernova rate within this region.

Department of Physics and Astronomy, McMaster University, Hamilton, ON L8S 4M1 Canada; schirmmr@mcmaster.ca, wilson@physics.mcmaster.ca Laboratoire AIM, CEA, Université Paris VII, IRFU/Service d’Astrophysique, Bat. 709, 91191 Gif-sur-Yvette, France Astrophysics Group, Imperial College, Blackett Laboratory, Prince Consort Road, London SW7 2AZ, UK

# Introduction

Merging and interacting galaxies play a fundamental role in the hierarchical evolution of galaxies (e.g. (cite: steinmetz2002)). In a major merger, the turbulent motion generated by the gravitational interaction between the two merging galaxies can lead to a significant increase in the star formation rate, usually in the form of starbursts (e.g. see (cite: hopkins2006) and references therein). For the most extreme mergers, this enhancement can culminate in an ultra luminous infrared galaxy (URLIG, $L_{IR} > 10^{12}$, (cite: sanders1996)). In fact, it has been shown that most, if not all, ULIRGs are the direct result of an ongoing merger (cite: sanders1988; sanders1996; clements1996).

In the nearby universe, the closest example of a major merger is the Antennae (NGC 4038/39, Arp 244), with the two progenitor galaxies, NGC 4038 and NGC 4039, still in a relatively early merger stage. Within this system, the region where the two initial gas disks are believed to overlap has been dubbed the “overlap region” (cite: stanford1990), while it has also been referred to as the “interaction region” (cite: schulz2007). Young, massive ($> 10^6 M_\odot$), compact “super star clusters” (SSCs) are found throughout the overlap region (cite: whitmore1999; whitmore2010). The overlap region also plays host to 5 super giant molecular complexes (SGMCs, (cite: wilson2000)), massive ($> 10^8 M_\odot$) associations of molecular gas within which current and future star formation is expected.

The molecular gas in the Antennae has been studied predominantly using the molecular gas tracer $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$, which is excited via collisions with $\mathrm{H_2}$. The total molecular gas content within the Antennae, assuming a Milky Way-like $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$-to-$\mathrm{H_2}$ conversion factor, is $\sim 2 \times
10^{10} \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{M_{\odot}}}$ (cite: gao2001). Interferometric observations of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ show the presence of 100 super giant molecular clouds (SGMCs) throughout the system with a mass range $\sim 10^7 - 10^9 M_\odot$(cite: wilson2003). More recently, (cite: schirm2014) analyzed observations of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ to $J=8-7$ using a non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) radiative transfer analysis. They found that most of the molecular gas in the system is cool ($T_{kin} \sim 10 - 30 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K}}$) and intermediately dense ($n(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H_2}}) \sim 10^3 - 10^4 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{cm^{-3}}}$), while a small fraction ($\sim 0.3 \%$) of the molecular gas is in a warm ($T_{kin} \gtrsim 100 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K}}$), dense ($n(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H_2}}) \gtrsim 10^4 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{cm^{-3}}}$) phase.

Recently, (cite: herrera2012) combined high-resolution Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) science verification observations of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=3-2$ in the Antennae with VLT/SINFONI imaging of the $\mathrm{H_2}$ $1-0 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{S(1)}}$ transition, while (cite: whitmore2014) obtained ALMA cycle-0 observations of the overlap region in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=3-2$. By combining their data with observations from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST), and the Very Large Array (VLA), (cite: whitmore2014) identify regions within the overlap region corresponding to the various stages of star formation, from diffuse giant molecular clouds (GMCs) all the way to intermediate and old stellar clusters. Of particular interest is the very bright $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=3-2$ emission found within SGMC 2, which (cite: whitmore2014) dubbed the “firecracker” and which is believed to be the precursor to a SSC. In addition, strong $\mathrm{H_2}$ $1-0 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{S(1)}}$ emission is associated with the bright $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=3-2$ emission (cite: herrera2012). The mass and energetics of the cloud suggest a very high pressure ($P/k_B \gtrsim 10^8 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K \ cm^{-3}}}$), while a lack of thermal radio emission indicates no star formation has yet occurred (cite: johnson2015).

While $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ is the most commonly used tracer of molecular gas, due to its brightness and relatively high abundance in giant molecular clouds (GMCs), it may not be the ideal tracer for the star forming molecular gas. Dense gas tracers, such as $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ (cite: gao2004a; gao2004b; papadopoulos2007), $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ (cite: talbi1996), and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ (cite: graciacarpio2006), can be used to study the molecular gas most directly linked to star formation. This relation culminates in the form of a tight relationship between the luminosity of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ ($L_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}}$) and the infrared (IR) luminosity ($L_{IR}$), tighter than the correlation between $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ and the infrared luminosity (cite: liu2010). In fact, this relationship holds in the form of a constant ratio of $L_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}}/L_{IR}$ from individual giant molecular clouds (GMCs) all the way up to luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs) (cite: wu2005). Recently, (cite: bigiel2015) used CARMA data to compare HCN and other dense tracers to the far-infrared luminosity to trace star formation efficiency and dense gas fraction. The critical densities of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ are all $n_{cr} > 10^5 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{cm^{-3}}}$ for the $J=1-0$ transition (cite: loenen2007), significantly higher than $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ ($n_{cr} \sim 3 \times 10^3 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{cm^{-3}}}$, (cite: loenen2007)).

Because $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ in the $J=1-0$ transition all have similar critical densities, the relative strengths of the lines of these molecules are driven largely by ongoing physical processes. Infrared (IR) pumping can enhance $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ emission in a system with a strong background mid-IR field (cite: sakamoto2010), while $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ can be destroyed via dissociative recombination in the presence of a significant abundance of electrons. $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$  are isotopomers, and their relative abundance is driven by the temperature of the dense molecular gas (cite: talbi1996). Line ratios of these molecules can be used as a diagnostic for cosmic rays (cite: meijerink2011), photon dominated regions (PDRs, (cite: kazandjian2012)), and mechanical heating (cite: loenen2008; kazandjian2012). Thus, these lines can be used to study the distribution of dense molecular gas within a system and to constrain the relative fraction of dense gas from region to region as well as the relative importance of physical processes such as mechanical heating.

In this paper, we present observations of the $J=1-0$ transition of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ in the Antennae using ALMA. We adopt a distance to NGC 4038/39 of $D = 22 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{Mpc}}$ (cite: schweizer2008), corresponding to an angular scale of $107 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{pc/''}}$.

We combine these observations with previous observations of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ from (cite: wilson2000; wilson2003). In this work, we detail the observations and data reduction in Section [2](#obsSect), while we discuss separating the emission into the brightest regions in Section [3](#brightSect). We present various line ratios of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ in Section [4](#lineRatSect), and we discuss the implications of the measured line ratios in Section [5](#discSect).

# Observations

NGC 4038 was observed in two pointings over the course of 2 nights each in March, 2013 and April, 2014 as part of ALMA Cycle-1. One pointing was positioned to cover the nucleus of NGC 4038 and the western loop ($12\ensuremath{\, \mathrm{h}}01\ensuremath{\, \mathrm{m}}51.7763\ensuremath{\, \mathrm{s}}, -18^{\circ}52'02.892''$), while the other was positioned to cover both the overlap region and the nucleus of NGC 4039 ($12\ensuremath{\, \mathrm{h}}01\ensuremath{\, \mathrm{m}}54.5945\ensuremath{\, \mathrm{s}}, -18^{\circ}52'50.891''$), with a total on-source integration time of $20356 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{seconds}}$. The antenna array configuration was C32-4. The bandpass calibrators used were J1256-0547, J1246-2547, and J1130-1449, while J1215-1731 was used as the phase calibrator and Titan was used as the amplitude calibrator throughout.

Band 3 was used, with one spectral window set to observe both $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ simultaneously. A second spectral window was aligned to search for $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$  emission throughout the Antennae. The total usable bandwidth for each of these spectral windows was $1875 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{MHz}}$ with a channel spacing of $0.488 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{MHz}}$. The two remaining spectral windows were centred at $101.0 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{GHz}}$ and $102.875 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{GHz}}$ to observe the continuum emission across the Antennae. The bandwidth of the two continuum windows was $2000\ensuremath{\, \mathrm{MHz}}$ with a channel spacing of $15.625 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{MHz}}$.

We reduce these data using the Common Astronomy Software Applications package version 4.2. We start by running the script provided to the PI as part of the data delivery in order to calibrate the *uv*-datasets before splitting out the target from the calibrated dataset. We further split out the spectral window which contains the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ lines, and the spectral window which contains the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ line. We subtract the background continuum emission by fitting a first order polynomial to the line-free channels of each spectral window using the `uvcontsub` task.

We create dirty data-cubes for each of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ $J=1-0$ transitions with a channel width of $5 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{km \ s^{-1}}}$ and cell size of $0.3''$. The restoring beams of the cleaned data cubes when using Briggs weighting with robust $= 0.5$ are $1.85'' \times 1.51'', -79.2^\circ$ for the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ line and $1.86'' \times 1.52'', -79.8^\circ$ for the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ line (the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ line was too weak to detect detect at the native ALMA resolution). We set the restoring beam for the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ transitions to the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ beam and create clean data-cubes by placing clean boxes around $>5\sigma$ emission in the dirty data-cubes, being careful not to select artifacts. We clean down to a threshold of $1.1 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{mJy \ beam^{-1}}}$, corresponding to $2\sigma$ in both dirty data cubes as measured in the line-free channels ($\sigma = 0.55 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{mJy \ beam^{-1}}}$).

In addition, we create dirty and clean data cubes to match the beam of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ data cube from (cite: wilson2000; wilson2003). We set the *uv*-taper on the outer baselines to $5.0''\times 2.0'', 1.45^\circ$ for $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ with a restoring beam of $4.91'' \times 3.15'', 1.45^\circ$. We use the same channel width and cell size as before, and draw clean boxes around $5\sigma$ emission. We clean down to a threshold of $1.6 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{mJy \ beam^{-1}}}$, corresponding to $2\sigma$ of the tapered dirty data cubes ($\sigma = 0.8 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{mJy \ beam^{-1}}}$).

We create moment maps including emission above $2\sigma$. The un-tapered moment 0 maps are shown in Figure [1](#denseOnHST), while the tapered moment 0 maps are shown in Figure [2](#denseOnCO), along with the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ moment 0 map from (cite: wilson2000; wilson2003). Finally, we correct all of our $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ moment-0 maps for the primary beam. The largest correction occurs in the nucleus of NGC 4039, where the primary beam correction is on the order of $\sim 0.6-0.7$ for both the native ALMA resolution maps and the $J=1-0$ resolution maps. The $J=1-0$ map from (cite: wilson2003) has already been corrected for the primary beam.

(cite: gao2001) observed the Antennae in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ $J=1-0$ in two pointings: one centered on the nucleus of NGC 4038, and the other on the brightest $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ emission from the overlap region. The full-width half-maximum of their beam was $\sim 72''$ and their two pointings include both nuclei and the overlap region. They calculate a total $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ $J=1-0$ luminosity of $0.8 \times 10^{8} \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K \ km \ s^{-1} \ pc^{2}}}$ (adjusted to our adopted distance of $22 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{Mpc}}$), while we measure a total of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ $J=1-0$ luminosity of $\sim 0.7 \times 10^{8} \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K \ km \ s^{-1} \ pc^{2}}}$ in our ALMA maps. Our detected $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ emission is well within their two beams, and we do not expect significant $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ emission outside of our observed region. This comparison suggests that we recover $\sim 90\%$ of the total $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ emission in our ALMA observations.

We estimate the measurement uncertainties in our moment maps by first determining the number of channels included in each pixel of the moment map ($N_{chan}$). We calculate the uncertainty in each pixel as $\sqrt{N_{chan}} \sigma \Delta v$, where $\sigma$ is the root-mean squared uncertainty measured from our line-free channels of our data cubes, and $\Delta v = 5 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{km/s}}$ is the channel width. Furthermore, when comparing our dense gas tracers to our $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$  $J=1-0$ map, we add a $5\%$ calibration uncertainty[^1]. The calibration uncertainty of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ map is $20 \%$ (cite: wilson2003). While individual luminosities can vary depending on the size of the aperture chosen, line ratio measured in the same apertures from maps with the same beam size should be quite accurate measures of the average line ratio over a given region. Line ratios involving the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ line may be somewhat more uncertain as this is the weakest line and so the 2$\sigma$ clipping used to make the moment maps is a larger fraction of the peak flux.

# The brightest regions in the Antennae

In this paper, we will focus on the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ emission from the brightest regions in the Antennae. A full catalogue of clouds in both $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ will be published in a future paper, along with a cloud-by-cloud analysis of the emission.

(cite: wilson2000) identified and isolated the 7 brightest regions in their $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ map of the Antennae using the clump identification algorithm CLFIND (cite: williams1994). These regions include both nuclei (NGC 4038 and NGC 4039), and 5 large clouds in the overlap region, dubbed Super Giant Molecular Complexes (SGMCs). In addition to these 7 regions, we identify two additional bright regions, C6 and C7. These clouds correspond to clouds 16, 17 and 18 (C6), and clouds 67 and 74 (C7) in the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ cloud catalogue published in (cite: wilson2003).

We place elliptical apertures around each of the 9 brightest regions to measure the total $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ fluxes ($S_{mol}$, Table [1](#fluxTab)) in the moment-0 map for the $J=1-0$ transition for each molecule (Figure [3](#regionsHCOonCO)). The total fluxes and total luminosities of the nuclei, SGMCs and clouds C6 and C7 are measured at the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ resolution for all 4 molecules.

For the 5 SGMC regions, we are unable to distinguish between SGMC 3, 4 and 5 in the moment-0 map and so we combine these three SGMCs into SGMC 3+4+5. We can, however, distinguish between them in velocity-space, as shown in (cite: wilson2000) (see their Figure 5). Using the measured local standard of rest velocity ($V_{lsr}$) along with the velocity widths ($\Delta V_{FWHM}$) from (cite: wilson2000), we create moment-0 maps for the velocity range spanned by each SGMC. We measure the flux and luminosity for each cloud in their own moment-0 map using the same aperture as used for SGMC 3+4+5. There are 2 channels of overlap in the velocity ranges for SGMC 4 and 5 as measured by (cite: wilson2000); we separate the two SGMCs by including one channel in each of the moment maps of SGMC 4 and 5.

(cite: johnson2015) identified a small region in SGMC 2 in their ALMA $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=3-2$ map of the overlap region which they believe to be the precursor to a super star cluster, which we have dubbed “pre-SSC” in this work. The resolution of their $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=3-2$ map is considerably better than that of our observations (beam size $= 0.56'' \times
0.43''$), while the size of pre-SSC as measured using the CPROPS program (cite: rosolowsky2006) is $\sim 0.66'' \times 0.55''$, less than the size of the beam of our $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ observations. We created a moment-0 map using the velocity range measured for the pre-SSC by (cite: johnson2015) and our data cubes at the native ALMA resolution. However, even in this map, the pre-SSC is not visible as a separate source. The $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ peak fluxes measured at the location of the pre-SSC are 0.28 and 0.45 Jy beam$^{-1}$ km s$^{-1}$, respectively; however, these fluxes almost certainly contain significant contamination from SGMC 2 and so should be regarded as upper limits to the true flux of the pre-SSC.
