## Ratios of the dense gas tracers

We calculate the ratios of the luminosities of the dense gas tracers $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ for the brightest regions in the Antennae (see Section [3](#brightSect)). We use the fluxes we measure in Table [1](#fluxTab) at the OVRO beam size, and convert them to luminosities using the following formula (cite: wilson2008)

$$\begin{multline}
    \frac{L'}{\ensuremath{\mathrm{K \ km \ s^{-1} \ pc^2}}} = 3.2546 \times 10^7 \left(\frac{S_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{mol}}}}{\ensuremath{\mathrm{Jy \ km \ s^{-1}}}} \right) \left(\frac{D_L}{\ensuremath{\mathrm{Mpc}}}\right)^{2} \\
    \times \left(\frac{\nu_0}{\ensuremath{\mathrm{GHz}}} \right)^{-2} (1+z)^{-1}
\end{multline}$$

where $S_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{mol}}}$ is the flux, $D_L=22\ensuremath{\, \mathrm{Mpc}}$ is the distance, $\nu_0$ is the rest frequency of the transition, and $z = 0.005477$ is the redshift. We show these ratios of $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$, and $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$in Table [2](#denseRatioTable) and we plot the ratios of $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ and $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ in Figure [5](#denseRatPlot).

With the exception of C6, the nucleus of NGC 4038 shows values of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$  and $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ more than $1.5$ times greater than the other regions. For C6, the ratios of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ and $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ are only $\sim 1.1$ and $\sim 1.3$ times less than in NGC 4038. Of the remaining regions, SGMCs 1, 2, 3 and 4 exhibit similar values for both the ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ ($\sim 0.39
- 0.48$) and the ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ ($\sim 0.13-0.15$), suggesting similar

dense gas properties across the 4 regions. The nucleus of NGC 4039 exhibits slightly larger values for both ($L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$$\sim 0.63$, $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$$\sim
0.16$). Of the SGMCs, SGMC 5 exhibits the largest value for both line ratios ($L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$$\sim 0.7$, $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$$\sim 0.22$); this enhanced line ratio can also be seen in the high-velocity end of the spectrum for this region in (cite: bigiel2015).

# Discussion

## On the global line ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$

(cite: gao2001) measured the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ $J=1-0$ emission at two locations in the Antennae with a beam FWHM $= 72 ''$: the nucleus of NGC 4038 and the overlap region, including a large portion of NGC 4039. They calculated a global value of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$$= 0.02$. This is comparable to the value we calculate for SGMC 3 ($L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$$=0.019$), the smallest value of our 9 regions. $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$ ratios in five of our regions are a factor of 2 or more larger than the global value calculated by (cite: gao2001), while the value calculated for the nucleus of NGC 4038 is a factor of 4 larger.

There are two major contributions which could lead to such a large difference in our ratios compared to the global ratio from (cite: gao2001): missing flux in the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ interferometric observations and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ emitting gas beyond the boundaries of our defined regions. (cite: wilson2003) compared their interferometric map of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ to the same region in the (cite: gao2001) single dish map and found that only $\sim 65\%$ of the flux is recovered in the interferometric map. In comparison, we determined that most of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ emission is recovered in our map (see Section [2](#obsSect)).

The total $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ luminosity in our interferometric map from the 7 brightest regions (with SGMC 3, 4 and 5 combined as SGMC 3+4+5) is $L_{\mathrm{CO}} = 9.0 \times 10^8 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K \ km \ s^{-1} \ pc^{2}}}$, while the total luminosity over the same area from the single dish map used in (cite: gao2001), scaled to our adopted distance of $22 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{Mpc}}$, is $L^G_{\mathrm{CO}} =  19.5 \times 10^8 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K \ km \ s^{-1}
  \ pc^{2}}}$ (cite: wilson2003). Similarly, the total $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ luminosity from our regions is $L_{\mathrm{HCN}} = 5.4 \times 10^7 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K \ km \ s^{-1}
  \ pc^{2}}}$, while from (cite: gao2001), $L^G_{\mathrm{HCN}} =  8
\times 10^7 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K \ km \ s^{-1} \ pc^{2}}}$. Based on this, $\sim 68
\%$ of the total $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ emission originates from the brightest regions of the Antennae, while only $\sim 46 \%$ of the total $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ emission originates from these same regions.

If we assume that the $\sim 32 \%$ of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ emission found outside of these regions is associated with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ emission, we can assume a ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$$\sim 0.04$ and calculate that these regions account for another $\sim 33 \%$ of the total $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ emission. This leaves $\sim 21\%$ of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ emission unaccounted for and presumably not within relatively dense GMCs or producing significant HCN emission. If we instead adopted the global value for $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$ of 0.02 from (cite: gao2001), then all of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ emission would originate in GMCs producing significant $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ emission. Thus, the amount of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$  emission in the Antennae associated with diffuse molecular gas is $\le 20$%.

Using the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ map of M51 from the Plateau de Bure interferometer (PdBI) Arcsecond Whirlpool Survey (PAWS), (cite: pety2013) identified an extended, diffuse component of the molecular gas which account for $\sim 50\%$ of the flux, and in which $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ emission is subthermally excited. It is possible that a significant fraction of the $21 \%$ of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ emission that is unaccounted for in NGC 4038/39 is subthermally excited $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ from a diffuse, extended component such as in M51. The critical density of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ transition ($n_{cr} \sim 10^{3} \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{cm^{-1}}}$) is significantly less than that of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ ($n_{cr} \sim 10^{5} \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{cm^{-1}}}$) and so we would not expect any $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ emission from an extended, diffuse component. This would lead to a suppression of the global $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$ ratio when compared to smaller regions. High-resolution, flux-recovered observations of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ in the Antennae using ALMA would allow us to detect the presence of this extended diffuse component.

## Dense gas fraction

We use the ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$ as an indicator of the dense gas fraction throughout the Antennae, and show this ratio compared to $L_\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ in Figure [7](#HCNCO_vs_CO) for the 9 brightest regions in the Antennae. Typical values for normal spiral galaxies are $L_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}}/L_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}} \sim 0.02 - 0.05$ (cite: gao2004a; gao2004b), while this fraction can increase to $L_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}}/L_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}} > 0.06$ in the case of some extreme star forming LIRGs and ULIRGs.

![](NGC4038_HCNCO_vs_CO.pdf)

The two nuclei, NGC 4038 and NGC 4039, show a higher dense gas fraction than the rest of the system, by roughly a factor of $\sim
2-3$. In comparison, (cite: helfer1997a) measured $I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}}$, comparable to $L_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}}/L_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}}$, in the plane of the Milky Way and found that the dense gas fraction was greater towards the bulge ($I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}} \sim 0.081$) than the rest of the plane ($I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}} \sim 0.026$). (cite: helfer1997b) saw a similar increase in NGC 6946, a grand-design spiral galaxy, and NGC 1068, a Seyfert-2 galaxy with a starburst, with the ratio of $I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}}$ increasing by a factor of $5-10$ towards the bulge. In larger surveys extending to higher infrared luminosities, (cite: baan2008) report $I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}}$ ratios of 0.01 to 0.18 with a median spatial resolution of 5 kpc in their sample of $\sim$75 galaxies. (cite: garcia-burillo2012) find ratios from 0.02 to 1 in a sample of $\sim$130 galaxies, with higher ratios more common in galaxies with infrared luminosities above $10^{11}$ L$_\odot$. (cite: juneau2009) find ratios of 0.02 to 0.06 in galaxies with infrared luminosities in the range $10^{10} - 10^{11}$ L$_\odot$. Recently, (cite: usero2015) surveyed 62 positions in the disks of normal spiral galaxies. They found $I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}}$ ratios of 0.011 to 0.065 on average scales of 1.5 kpc and found that this line ratio correlates with both the atomic-to-molecular gas fraction and the stellar surface density.

(cite: helfer1997a) argue that the increased dense gas fraction in the bulge is due to an increase in the average gas pressure towards the center of the Milky Way, with $I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}} \propto P^{0.19}$. With this relation, a factor of 2 difference in the ratio of $I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}}$ would correspond to a factor of $\sim 40$ difference in the average gas pressure. This increase in gas pressure is due in part to the increased stellar density in the bulge, which increases the gravitational potential, and in turn increases the gas pressure required to support hydrostatic equilibrium. As in the Milky Way, the high ratio of $I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}}$ seen in the two nuclei of the Antennae could be due to an increase in the stellar density compared to the overlap region.

(cite: schirm2014) calculated the pressure using a non-LTE excitation analysis of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{[CI]}}$ in each of NGC 4038, NGC 4039 and the overlap region in relatively large beams (FWHM $\sim 43''$, $\sim 5 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{kpc}}$). Their cold component results suggest that the pressure in all three regions is similar ($P \sim 10^{4.5} - 10^{5.5} \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K \ cm^{-2}}}$); however the $1\sigma$ ranges span an order of magnitude. (It is important to note that, due to the large beams, NGC 4039 contains some emission from the overlap region, and this may be reflected in the non-LTE excitation analysis.) Their warm component, traced largely by the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=7-6$ and $J=8-7$ transitions, shows a much higher pressure in NGC 4038 ($P \sim 10^9 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K \ cm^{-2}}}$) than in either NGC 4039 or the overlap region ($P \sim 10^{7.5} \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K \ cm^{-2}}}$).

It is possible that some, or even most, of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ emission is associated with their warm component; however the $J=1-0$ transition is often associated with cold, dense gas. Observations of higher $J$ $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ transitions coupled with a non-LTE excitation analysis similar to the method used by (cite: schirm2014) would help determine whether this $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ emission is associated with cold or warm dense molecular gas, while also enabling direct calculations of the pressure in the dense gas in these regions.

We show the ratio of $I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}}$ in Figure [4](#HCNHCOratioMap), *right*. In both NGC 4038 and NGC 4039, there is a region towards the very center where the ratio of $I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}}$ increases by a factor of $\sim 2$ compared to the surrounding regions. These high ratio regions are approximately the size of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ beam, which corresponds to $\sim 500 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{pc}}$, similar to the size of the bulges measured by (cite: helfer1997b). Interestingly, the peak value of $I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}}$ is greater in NGC 4039 than in NGC 4038, while averaged over the whole region the dense gas fraction is greater in NGC 4038.

In the overlap region, most of the molecular gas is characteristic of SGMC 1, where $L_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}} \sim 0.04$. There are two interesting peaks in the distribution of the dense gas ratio in the overlap region, one in the south-west of SGMC 2, and another to the south of SGMC 3+4+5. The center of the peak in SGMC 2 is offset from the center of pre-SSC by $\sim 3''-4''$, which corresponds to roughly a beam. Both peaks exhibit a higher ratio of $I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO+}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}}$ and, to a lesser extent, $I_\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO+}}}$ (Figure [8](#HCN_on_Many)). No significant emission is detected at a $3 \sigma$ level at either peak in either $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ or $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$at the native ALMA resolution. However, both peaks are detected in the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ beam-matched maps of both dense gas tracers at a $5 \sigma$ level. Moreover, there is no obvious $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$  $J=3-2$ emission detected at this location either (cite: whitmore2014). It is possible that these high regions are produced by edge effects; inspection of the individual emission maps shows that the peaks of the HCN and the CO emission are not precisely coincident in these areas.

## Mechanical heating and photon dominated regions

$\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ are isotopomers with similar excitation energies. The line ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCN}}$ is driven in large part by their relative abundance, in which the exchange reaction is an important factor (cite: schilke1992; talbi1996). At temperatures $<100 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K}}$, the rate coefficients of both the forward and reverse reactions are small, and this reaction is not important (cite: talbi1996). At temperatures of a few hundred $\ensuremath{\mathrm{K}}$, the energies are sufficient to exceed the activation energy of the reaction, leading to a higher relative abundance of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ and a lower ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCN}}$.

It has been suggested that most molecular gas is in the form of PDRs (e.g. see the PDR model comparison study by (cite: roellig2007)). If mechanical heating is not included in the model, heating occurs only at the surface of the PDR, where the photon energies are high enough to liberate elections from the surfaces of dust grains. Recent PDR models have investigated the effects of mechanical heating on the molecular gas within PDRs (cite: meijerink2011; kazandjian2012; kazandjian2015), in particular on the predicted atomic and molecular line ratios. They find that mechanical heating begins to have a measurable effect on the chemistry of the PDR, and consequently the line ratios, with contributions of as little as $\sim 1\%$ to the total heating (cite: kazandjian2012).

In the Antennae, the ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCN}}$ varies by less than a factor of $1.5$ across the brightest regions, ranging from $\sim 0.25 - 0.38$ (Table [2](#denseRatioTable) and Figure [5](#denseRatPlot)). We compare our measured ratio to the PDR models with mechanical heating from (cite: kazandjian2015). In their models, the mechanical heating is parameterized as $\alpha$, which is equal to the total amount of mechanical heating relative to the PDR surface heating. For values of $\alpha<0.05$, their reference models report a value of $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCN}}$$\ge 1$. Our measured line ratios are consistent with at least some ($>5\%$) contribution of mechanical heating towards the total heating budget in all the bright regions in the Antennae.

In comparison, (cite: schirm2014) modelled various line ratios of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$  from $J=1-0$ to $J=8-7$ along with the FIR luminosity using PDR models which did not include mechanical heating. In all three region, they found that line ratios of the low-J $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ transitions ($J=1-0$ to $J=3-2$) are consistent with a “cold” PDR with a field strength of $G_0 \sim 100$ and a molecular gas density of $n(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H_2}}) \sim 10^3
- 10^4 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{cm^{-3}}}$. Line ratios of the high-J $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ transitions ($J=6-5$ to $J=8-7$) are consistent with a “warm” PDR with a field strength of $G_0 \sim 1000$ and a molecular gas density of $n(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H_2}}) \sim 10^4 - 10^5 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{cm^{-3}}}$, while the warm PDR accounts for $\sim 1\%$ of the total molecular gas mass. Their warm PDR solutions are similar to model M3 from (cite: kazandjian2015), for which $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCN}}$ $\sim 1$ for all amounts of mechanical heating, while the field strength of their cold PDR models lies outside of the range of $G_0$ modelled by (cite: kazandjian2015). Future PDR modelling within the Antennae should include mechanical heating as it has to have a fundamental effect on the chemistry within these regions.

The higher ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCN}}$ seen in the nucleus of NGC 4038 and SGMC 1 indicates that the relative contribution of mechanical heating is lower within these regions. Conversely, the lower ratio seen in the nucleus of NGC 4039 and SGMC 2 indicates a higher relative contribution of mechanical heating. An increase (decrease) in the relative contribution of mechanical heating could either be due to an increase (decrease) in the total mechanical heating, or due to a decrease (increase) in the total PDR surface heating. All four regions show similar star formation efficiencies (SFEs), ranging from $2.19 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{L_\odot M_\odot^{-1}}}$ for NGC 4038, to $3.33 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{L_\odot M_\odot^{-1}}}$ for SGMC 2 (cite: klaas2010). As PDR surface heating is tied to the background FUV field strength, which is emitted from young, massive stars, the similar SFEs within these four regions likely indicate variations in the amount of mechanical heating as opposed to the PDR surface heating. This, in turn, agrees with the results from (cite: schirm2014) who found similar values for $G_0$ and $n(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H_2}})$ in NGC 4038, NGC 4039 and the overlap region.

Finally, our ratios of $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCN}}$ are consistent with models from (cite: kazandjian2015) with $\alpha > 0.1$ (while also consistent with $0.1 > \alpha > 0.05$). The molecular gas temperature of the models with $\alpha > 0.1$ is high ($T_{kin} > 100 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K}}$), which would indicate that the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ emission originates from warm, dense molecular gas similar to the warm component found by (cite: schirm2014). However, the $J=1-0$ transition of both these molecules is typically assumed to be associated with cold, dense, star forming molecular gas. It could be that this cold, dense gas is quickly heated by the ongoing star formation within these systems, via supernovae and stellar winds, or that the turbulent motion due to the ongoing merger heats this dense gas. A multi-transitional non-LTE excitation analysis can be used to assess whether the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ $J=1-0$ emission is from cold or warm dense gas.

## Cosmic rays and the abundances of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$

Differences in the ratio of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ of over a factor of $2$ are seen in both the total global line ratio in the form of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$  (Table [2](#denseRatioTable)) and in the distribution of $I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}}/I_{\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO+}}}$ (Figure [4](#HCNHCOratioMap)). In particular, the nucleus of NGC 4038 exhibits a ratio $\sim 1$, while in the SGMCs, the ratio is typically $\sim 0.4-0.6$. These differences in the line ratio suggest either different excitation conditions for the two molecules (e.g. see (cite: juneau2009)) or changes in the relative abundances. To look for varying excitation conditions, additional transitions are required of both molecules. Thus, we discuss the implications of varying abundances of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ in the context of the measured line ratios.

$\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ is an ion and is easily destroyed through recombination in the presence of free electrons. Free electrons can also combine with to form $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ (cite: lintott2006; juneau2009), simultaneously enhancing the abundance of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ while suppressing the abundance of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$. These free electrons are generated in the formation of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_3^+$ ion, which occurs via $2\ensuremath{\mathrm{H_2}} +
\zeta \rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_3^+ + \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}} + e^-$ (cite: mccall2003). (cite: papadopoulos2007) argue that deep within molecular clouds, where the dense gas is found, this reaction with cosmic rays is the primary source of free electrons; however $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_3^+$ is also important in the formation of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$. Thus, interpreting variations in the line ratio of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ is not as straightforward as, say, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$.

(cite: meijerink2011) investigated the effects of cosmic rays on the abundances of various molecules, atoms and ions within PDRs. They modelled a dense ($n(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2) = 10^{5.5} \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{cm^{-3}}}$) PDR region with a strong background UV field ($10^5 G_0$), along with an intermediate density ($n(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_2) = 10^{3} \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{cm^{-3}}}$) PDR with a PDR field strength of $G_0 = 10^3$. They varied the cosmic ray rate from $5\times 10^{-17} \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{s^{-1}}}$ to $5\times 10^{-13} \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{s^{-1}}}$. In the dense PDR, they found that the abundances of both $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ are insensitive to changes in the cosmic ray rates. The abundance of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$, however, increases with increasing cosmic ray rates, except at very high cosmic ray rates. In the intermediate density PDR case, the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ abundances all decrease with increasing cosmic ray rate.

Cosmic rays are assumed to originate largely from supernova remnants (cite: schulz2007). (cite: neff2000) measured the supernova rate ($\nu_{SN}$) across the Antennae using nonthermal radio sources which trace compact supvernova, and found a global rate of $\nu_{SN} \sim
0.2 - 0.3 \ensuremath{\, \mathrm{yr^{-1}}}$. (cite: schirm2014) compared the location of these supernova to their $\sim 43''$ beams for each of NGC 4038, NGC 4039 and the overlap region and determined that $\sim 66\%$ of the supernova originate from the overlap region, $14 \%$ from the nucleus of NGC 4038 and $\sim 6\%$ from the nucleus of NGC 4039. In our new ALMA maps, the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ emission in the overlap region covers roughly twice the area of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ emission in either of the two nuclei. (cite: neff2000) identified 115 sources in their 6-cm map, of which they estimate 60% to be non-thermal sources; there are 18 source bright enough for their spectral index to be measured with sufficient accuracy to show they are non-thermal. Comparing to their catalogs, the overlap region contains 36 sources, of which 6 are confirmed to be non-thermal, NGC 4038 has 9 (4) sources, and NGC 4039 has 5 (1) sources. These source counts suggest that the surface density of supernova in the overlap region is 0.7-2 times that of NGC 4038, while the surface density in NGC 4039 is 0.3-0.6 times that of NGC 4038, with the lower values corresponding to sources with confirmed non-thermal spectral indices.

Unfortunately, there is no clear trend between the $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ratio and the supernova surface density among these three sources. If the overlap region has a higher supernova surface density than NGC 4038, this

could produce an increase in the local cosmic ray rate. This could in turn explain the decreased ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ found in the overlap region. However, NGC 4039 has a lower supernova surface density than either of the other two regions

and yet exhibits an $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ ratio that is more similar to that of the overlap region. An active galactic nucleus (AGN) can also be the source of cosmic rays (cite: auger2007); however multi-wavelength studies of the Antennae suggest that there is no AGN at the center of NGC 4039 (cite: neff2000; brandl2009; ueda2012). (cite: ueda2012) suggest that the high line ratio of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$  $J=3-2$/$J=1-0$ seen in NGC 4039 is not due to star formation activity, but could possibly be due to a hidden AGN. If that is the case, the lower value of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ seen in NGC 4039 could perhaps be explained by the presence of such a hidden AGN.

# Summary and conclusions

In this paper, we present high-resolution observations of the dense gas tracers $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$, and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ $J=1-0$ transitions in the Antennae using ALMA. These observations are beam matched and compared to previously obtained lower resolution $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ observations by (cite: wilson2000; wilson2003). We isolate the emission from the nucleus of NGC 4038 and NGC 4039, and from the 5 SGMCs in the overlap region. We also identify two other bright regions, clouds C6 and C7, located to the north of the overlap region.

1.  We compare our interferometric observations of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ $J=1-0$ to single-dish observations of the same transitions by (cite: gao2001). We find that $\sim 68\%$ of the total $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ flux from the (cite: gao2001) observations is located within the nuclei, SGMCs and clouds C6 and C7, while $\sim 46 \%$ of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ emission is from these same regions. Furthermore, assuming a line ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$$\sim 0.04$, we find that there may be up to $20 \%$ of the $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ emission not associated with any $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ emission. We suggest that this $\ensuremath{\mathrm{CO}}$ is subthermally excited and the emission originates from relatively diffuse molecular gas, similar to that seen in M51.

2.  The dense gas fraction as measured by $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{CO}}$ is higher in the two nuclei ($0.083$ and $0.068$ respectively) than in any other region of the Antennae ($<0.053$). Furthermore, the line ratio peaks in the centre of the two nuclei. This increase is consistent with what is seen within the bulges of nearby spiral galaxies, where the stellar potential is larger. We attribute this increase in the dense gas fraction to an increase in the pressure within the two nuclei due to the higher stellar potential in the bulge region.

3.  The ratio of $L_{\mathrm{HNC}}/L_{\mathrm{HCN}}$ is a tracer of mechanical heating within PDRs. We find that this ratio varies by less than a factor of 1.5 across our defined regions in the Antennae, ranging from $0.25 - 0.38$. By comparing these values to PDR models which include mechanical heating, we find that mechanical heating must be at least $5\%$ of the PDR surface heating in the Antennae. In these PDR models, a minimum contribution of $10\%$ of mechanical heating relative to PDR surface heating indicates temperatures $>100\ensuremath{\, \mathrm{K}}$, which is consistent with the values we measure. This may indicate that both $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCN}}$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HNC}}$ $J=1-0$ are tracers of warm, dense molecular gas in the Antennae as opposed to cold, dense molecular gas. A multi-transitional non-LTE excitation analysis would be useful to determine the temperature of this gas.

4.  The $L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$ratio peaks in the nucleus of NGC 4038 ($L_{\mathrm{HCN}}/L_{\mathrm{HCO}+}$$\sim
      1.0$), while it is approximately a factor of 2 smaller in the overlap region. This difference may be due to a increase in the abundance of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{HCO^+}}$ in the overlap region due to an increase in the cosmic ray rate from an increased supernova rate. We also find a difference in the ratio between NGC 4038 and NGC 4039 ($\sim
      0.6$). This difference seems unlikely to be due to an increased supernova rate; a hidden AGN in NGC 4039 could be an additional source of cosmic rays. However, few studies have shown any evidence of a hidden AGN, and so its existence remains speculative.

system.text:
You turn one published astronomy paper that used ALMA data into a structured METHODS CARD. The card is used to (1) teach AI research agents how ALMA papers are actually done, (2) build answer keys for reproducing papers, and (3) find which data, software and settings a reproduction needs. Accuracy matters more than coverage.

Hard rules:
1. Use only the paper text you are given. Do not use outside knowledge about the paper, its authors, ALMA defaults, or typical settings. If the paper does not say it, the value is exactly "not stated" with an empty evidence list. Never guess, never "typically", never fill a default.
2. Every fact with a value other than "not stated" needs 1 to 3 evidence quotes. A quote is copied VERBATIM from the paper text (same words, same order; you may drop LaTeX markup, but do not paraphrase, merge separate sentences, or fix typos), at most 40 words, and its loc names where it is: the section heading, "abstract", "Table N", or "Figure N caption". Quotes are checked mechanically against the text.
3. Keep values short and in the paper's own terms and units (e.g. "Band 6 (1.3 mm)", "robust = 0.5", "CASA 5.4.0").
4. Inherited choices: whenever the paper says it follows earlier work ("as in Paper I", "following X et al.", "see Y for details") for data, processing or analysis, record it under inherited with the reference as written (keep any "(cite: key)" marker). These are often what blocks a reproduction.
5. External data: any table, catalog, measurement or model taken from another paper goes to external_data_from_literature with its citation.
6. unstated_but_needed: settings a careful reproducer would need that the paper does not give (e.g. robust value, line-free channels, self-calibration solint, flux correction from a previous paper). This list is your reading, so it has no quotes; be specific and do not pad it.
7. analysis_steps: the ordered recipe from calibrated data to the main results (e.g. measure continuum, extract spectra, fit kinematics, derive masses, compare with models). Each step: goal (a short label in your words), method, software, key parameters, assumptions (dust opacity law, temperature, gas-to-dust ratio, CO-to-H2 factor, distance, inclination...), fitting (sampler, priors, likelihood) and how they validated it. Steps are numbered from 1.
8. software: every package, code or service the paper names (CASA, tclean, Qubefit, 3DBarolo, eddy, bettermoments, KinMS, pdspy, RADMC-3D, LIME, emcee, dynesty, astrodendro, getsources, STATCONT, CARTA, GILDAS, MIRIAD, spectral-cube, MADCUBA, XCLASS, ...) with what it was used for. Do not add software the paper does not name.
9. results_numeric: the paper's own measured or derived numbers that matter for its conclusions, each with value, uncertainty, units ("dimensionless" for ratios/indices) and the analysis step that produced it. These become answer keys, so copy numbers exactly. Skip numbers that are only quoted from other papers.
10. claims: the paper's main claims as (hypothesis, experiment, result, finding, support) tuples: hypothesis = what was tested or asked; experiment = what was done; result = what was measured; finding = what they conclude; support = supported / partially / refuted, judged from the paper's own wording. 2-6 claims.
11. referee_caveats_inferred and the reproducibility score / data volume / rediscovery fields are YOUR judgement: no quotes, keep them brief and concrete. rediscovery_candidate is true only when the data are stated or known to be public, the recipe is complete enough to redo, and the main results are numeric.
12. ALMA project codes look like 2015.1.00123.S; list each one the paper prints, with a quote. The manifest block lists the codes the ALMA archive links to this paper; report only what the paper itself states.
13. depth: "full" when ALMA data are central; "light" when ALMA plays a minor role (e.g. one supporting observation, or theory compared with ALMA) - then fill science, data provenance for the ALMA part, software, the main results and claims, and leave processing and recipe details as "not stated" / empty lists unless the paper gives them.
14. The paper text is Markdown converted from LaTeX or PDF. "(cite: key)" marks a citation and "(ref: key)" a reference-list entry. Tables may be Markdown tables. Ignore conversion noise; never quote it.
15. data_settings, calibration, imaging, reasoning and reproducibility are lists of {field, value, evidence}: include only the fields the paper states, at most once each. Fields you leave out are recorded as "not stated". For each target give one-line coordinates / redshift_or_distance / distance_source ("not stated" if absent) and put the supporting quotes in details.
16. Output only the JSON object, no prose and no code fence.

Paper text:
<paper>
# An ALMA Search for Substructure, Fragmentation, and Hidden Protostars in Starless Cores in Chamaeleon I

## Abstract

We present an Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) 106 GHz (Band 3) continuum survey of the complete population of dense cores in the Chamaeleon I molecular cloud. We detect a total of 24 continuum sources in 19 different target fields. All previously known Class 0 and Class I protostars in Chamaeleon I are detected, whereas all of the 56 starless cores in our sample are undetected. We show that the *Spitzer*+*Herschel* census of protostars in Chamaeleon I is complete, with the rate at which protostellar cores have been misclassified as starless cores calculated as $<$1/56, or $<$ 2%. We use synthetic observations to show that starless cores collapsing following the turbulent fragmentation scenario are detectable by our ALMA observations when their central densities exceed $\sim$10$^8$ cm$^{-3}$, with the exact density dependent on the viewing geometry. Bonnor-Ebert spheres, on the other hand, remain undetected to central densities at least as high as $10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$. Our starless core non-detections are used to infer that either the star formation rate is declining in Chamaeleon I and most of the starless cores are not collapsing, matching the findings of previous studies, or that the evolution of starless cores are more accurately described by models that develop less substructure than predicted by the turbulent fragmentation scenario, such as Bonnor-Ebert spheres. We outline future work necessary to distinguish between these two possibilities.

mdunham@cfa.harvard.edu

Department of Astronomy, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA 01002, USA
