To further explore the dust content of II Zw 40, we have added the mid- and far-infrared Herschel photometry and resulting fit from (cite: 2013A&A...557A..95R) to the ALMA and VLA data points to better capture the peak of the dust emission (Figure [11](#fig:cont_sed_dust)). To obtain an estimate of the dust mass from these points, we attempted to fit a modified black body to the dust emission: $$\begin{equation}
  F_\nu = \frac{M_{dust} \kappa (\lambda_0)}{D^2}
  \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_0}\right)^{-\beta} B_\nu(\lambda,T)
\end{equation}$$ where $M_{dust}$ is the dust mass, $\kappa(\lambda_0)$ is the dust absorption coefficient at the reference wavelength $\lambda_0$, $D$ is distance to the object, $\lambda$ is the observed wavelength, $\beta$ is the dust emissivity index, and $B_\nu(\lambda,T)$ is the Planck function. We assume a value for $\kappa(\lambda_0)$ of 4.5 ${\rm m^2 \, kg^{-1}}$. This value is based on the models of (cite: 2004ApJS..152..211Z) and is the same value used in (cite: 2013A&A...557A..95R). All attempts to fit a modified blackbody through both the ALMA and Herschel data points yielded poor fits. The failure of these fits is most likely due to either large-scale dust emission being resolved out by ALMA or to the large difference between the apertures used for the Herschel and ALMA photometry: 132$''$ versus 9$''$. Although we could increase the aperture size for the ALMA data, the Herschel aperture is larger than our ALMA field of view (see Table [4](#tab:image_summary_cont)).

Given our inability to fit both the ALMA and Herschel points simultaneously, we derive an estimate of the dust mass using only the ALMA data by setting $\beta$ and the temperature to the values derived by (cite: 2013A&A...557A..95R): 1.71 and 33K. We obtain a dust mass of $(1.8\pm0.2) \times 10^4 \ \ensuremath{\rm{M}_\odot}$, which is a factor of 10 less than the dust mass estimated by (cite: 2013A&A...557A..95R): $1.9 \times 10^5 \ \ensuremath{\rm{M}_\odot}$. We note that fixing the $\beta$ value only has a minor effect on the derived mass. Changing $\beta$ from 1.71 to 2.0 changes the mass by less than 10%. In addition, since our observations are on the Raleigh-Jeans tail of the dust distribution, our derived dust mass is only minimally affected by the assumed temperature: the mass-weighted temperature would need to have a factor of two uncertainty to produce a factor of two uncertainty in the mass .

![](cont_sed_vla_alma_herschel_nat_uvtaper_1arcsec-eps-converted-to.pdf)

Armed with a dust mass for II Zw 40, we can calculate its gas-to-dust ratio ($\delta_{GDR}$), which links the gas and dust content within the galaxy. The gas-to-dust ratio is used as an alternative way to trace the molecular gas content of a galaxy (cite: 1997A&A...328..471I; 2011ApJ...737...12L; 2013ApJ...777....5S). Here we use archival VLA neutral hydrogen data (cite: 1998AJ....116.1186V) and the molecular gas measurements from Section [\[sec:coh-ratio-molecular\]](#sec:coh-ratio-molecular) to calculate the gas-to-dust ratio in II Zw 40 and compare it to theoretical estimates of the gast-to-dust ratio in low metalllicity systems.

The gas-to-dust ratio is defined as $$\begin{equation}
  \ensuremath{\delta_{GDR}}= \frac{\ensuremath{\alpha_{co}}\ensuremath{{\rm L_{CO}}}+ M_{HI} }{M_{dust}}
\end{equation}$$ where $\ensuremath{\alpha_{co}}$ is the CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor in $\ensuremath{\rm M_\odot (\ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}})^{-1}}$, $\ensuremath{{\rm L_{CO}}}$ is the CO luminosity in $\ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}}$, and $M_{HI}$ and $M_{dust}$ are the neutral hydrogen and dust masses, respectively, in $\rm{M}_\odot$. Here we are defining $\delta_{GDR}$ in terms of masses, instead of surface densities, which requires us to match the apertures used to measure each quantity. In the same 9$''$ aperture as we used to measure the continuum SED, we measure an $M_{HI}$ of $6.0\times10^6$ $\rm{M}_\odot$ and a $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ luminosity of $2.1 \times 10^5$ $\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}$, which corresponds to a $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ luminosity of $3.8 \times 10^5$ $\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}$ using an ${\rm r_{31}}$ value of 0.54. From § [\[sec:coh-ratio-molecular\]](#sec:coh-ratio-molecular), we have estimates from $\alpha_{co}$ that range from 18.1 $\rm M_\odot (\ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}})^{-1}$ to 150.5 $\rm M_\odot (\ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}})^{-1}$. These values give a range for $\delta_{GDR}$ of 720 to 3500. We note that, if we are resolving out a significant amount of continuum emission, our $\delta_{GDR}$ will be overestimates (because we will have underestimated the dust content). The lower end of our estimated range range is similar to the (cite: 2014A&A...563A..31R) predicted value (645-660, depending on assumptions about $\alpha_{co}$). It is greater than, but still within an order of magnitude, of the $\delta_{GDR}$ predicted by the (cite: 2011ApJ...737...12L) (330) and the range of values given for blue compact dwarfs of similar metallicity by (cite: 2014A&A...561A..49H). We do not see any evidence for the dichotomy seen in Hunt et al. for the $\delta_{GDR}$ ratios for the very low metallicity galaxies I Zw 18 and SBS0335-052, although the metallicity of II Zw 40 is ten times higher than in both of those systems.

## The Molecular Clouds Fueling the Starburst within II Zw 40

[^1]: Note that Figure 2 in (cite: 2014AJ....147...43K) does not show the entire field of view for these observations.

[^2]: The size of the single dish beam is 11$''$, which is comparable to the largest angular scale observed by ALMA in this image.

Observations of low metallicity galaxies with the spatial and spectral resolutions necessary to resolve individual molecular clouds are rare because of the faint nature of the CO emission in these galaxies. Previously, only a dozen or so galaxies had bright enough CO to obtain high resolution observations with sufficient signal to noise, e.g., Table 1 in (cite: 2008ApJ...686..948B). These galaxies were typically limited either to very nearby galaxies or to those with relatively high metallicities (and thus brighter CO). The sensitivity and resolution of ALMA observations, like those presented here for II Zw 40, allow us to measure for the resolved molecular cloud properties in fainter and more extreme low metallicity systems, and compare them to the properties of molecular clouds in other galaxies.

Originally motivated by observations in the Milky Way (cite: 1981MNRAS.194..809L; 1987ApJ...319..730S), the so-called Larson’s laws are commonly used to quantify and compare the giant molecular cloud properties in galaxies. The first relationship states that the linewidth of a molecular cloud scales with its size and is generally referred to as the size-linewidth relationship. The second relationship shows that the CO luminosity of a molecular cloud is correlated with its virial mass. This relationship is typically used to infer the conversion factor between the observed CO luminosity and the molecular gas mass of a cloud, under the assumptions that virial equilibrium holds and that the CO traces the full extent of the molecular gas. The final relationship, which is a consequence of the first two, states that molecular clouds all have approximately the same surface density. These relationships have been shown to be sensitive to the resolution and sensitivity limits of the data and the methods used to measure the cloud properties (cite: 2011ApJS..197...16W; 2013ApJ...779...46H). However, they continue to provide the basic framework for understanding giant molecular cloud populations.

In this section, we identify individual molecular clouds within II Zw 40, quantify their properties, and compare these properties to those of molecular clouds in other environments. Our comparison sample was selected to span a wide range of cloud properties and environments. It includes cloud samples from the Milky Way disk (cite: 2009ApJ...699.1092H), the center of the Milky Way (cite: 2001ApJ...562..348O), the nearby low metallicity irregular Large Magellanic Cloud (cite: 2011ApJS..197...16W), the Local Group dwarf starburst IC 10 (cite: 2006ApJ...643..825L), the major merger referred to as the Antennae ((cite: 2014ApJ...795..156W), Leroy et al. in prep), and the nuclear starburst galaxy NGC 253 (cite: 2015ApJ...801...25L). To mitigate the effects of varying sensitivity and resolution, we have focused on comparison cloud samples whose original observations have relatively high ($\lesssim 50$pc) resolution and good surface brightness sensitivity and where the algorithms used to determine the cloud properties were similar to those used here, i.e., variants on the algorithm in (cite: 2006PASP..118..590R).

### Measuring the Cloud Properties

We used the cprops algorithm (cite: 2006PASP..118..590R) to identify individual molecular clouds within II Zw 40 and calculate their properties. This algorithm identifies significant emission within a cube using a dilated mask and associates this emission with individual clouds using a modified watershed algorithm. The $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ data cube was used to identify the clouds because it has the highest signal-to-noise out of all our data sets. To identify significant emission, we used a three dimensional noise cube and required the emission to be greater than 5$\sigma$ in two adjacent channels to generate an initial mask. All pixels connected to this initial mask down to a 2$\sigma$ level were then added to the mask. To decompose the emission into individual clouds, we used a box of 0.35$''$ by 0.35$''$ by 6 $\rm{km \, s}^{-1}$; 0.35$''$ is 17pc at the adopted distance of II Zw 40. We rejected regions with a contrast less than 1.5$\sigma$ and areas less than the FWHM of the beam. We note that emission that can be associated with more than one cloud is not included in the mask. The measured cloud properties have been extrapolated down to 0K and corrected for the angular and velocity resolution of the data as described in (cite: 2006PASP..118..590R).

Our results do not depend strongly on the cube used for the decomposition, decomposition algorithm, or decomposition parameters. The cube decompositions for both the $\rm{^{12} CO ({2}-{1})}$ and $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ both identify the brightest clouds. The main difference between the two cloud identifications is that the $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ emission spans a larger continuous area at high signal to noise; the $\rm{^{12} CO ({2}-{1})}$ emission appears to be moderately clumpier because only the brightest peaks remain at high signal to noise. An alternative decomposition algorithm – clumpfind (cite: 1994ApJ...428..693W) – produces similar results when applied to our data to those generated by the cprops algorithm. Finally, changing the decomposition parameters only affects how many clouds the main molecular ridge is separated into. Depending on the parameters chosen, the ridge can either be identified as a single large cloud or up to four different clouds. We have tuned these parameters to match the number of clumps that can be distinguished by eye in the position-velocity plot of the $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ emission (Figure [1](#fig:cprops_clumps)).

The cloud identifications are shown in Figure [1](#fig:cprops_clumps) overlaid on the $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ data and the cloud properties in Table [\[tab:gmc_props\]](#tab:gmc_props). Since the clouds are largely Gaussian, the final cloud sizes and luminosities (and thus their associated properties like mass, etc) were taken from the Gaussian fit to the cloud sizes with the beam and channel width deconvolved. For clouds that were unresolved, we derive an upper limit on the radius of the cloud by calculating the diameter of a circle that has the same area as the area at half-maximum covered by the cloud.

![](co32_mom8_pv_cprops-eps-converted-to.pdf)

Monte Carlo simulations were used to determine the errors on the measured properties. We added Gaussian noise with the same properties as the noise cube used to mask the emission to the image cube and calculated the properties of the resulting clumps. After 100 iterations, we calculated the standard deviation of the resulting clump properties and used this value as the error. For flux-related values, we added the errors on the derived flux (10% at 870$\mu$m and 20% at 1 mm; see Section [\[sec:data\]](#sec:data)) in quadrature with the errors derived from the Monte Carlo simulations.

In the literature, the $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ transition is the most common tracer of molecular gas. To compare our data to the $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ data in the literature, we scale our $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ emission for all clouds, except cloud G, to the expected $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ value using a 10K blackbody, which is consistent with the line ratios for the entire galaxy (see Section [\[sec:overview-data\]](#sec:overview-data)). Since cloud G has a significantly different value of ${\rm r_{32}}$, we scale its $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ emission to the expected $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ value using a 6K blackbody, which is consistent with the ratio seen in that cloud (again see Section [\[sec:overview-data\]](#sec:overview-data)).

### The CO-to-H$_2$ Conversion Factor

Since CO is used as the primary tracer of molecular gas beyond the Local Group, quantifying the relationship between CO emission and the amount of molecular gas in different environments is key for understanding the role of molecular gas in star formation throughout cosmic time. In the Milky Way, this conversion factor is typically 4.3 $\rm M_\odot (\ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}})^{-1}$ (cite: 2013ARA&A..51..207B). However, it is a factor of $\sim5$ lower in starburst galaxies like LIRGs and ULIRGs and several times higher in low metallicity systems (cite: 2013ARA&A..51..207B). As detailed in the introduction, the high $\alpha_{co}$ values in the latter systems are due to reduced dust shielding for the CO (cite: 2008ApJ...686..948B; 2011ApJ...737...12L). In contrast, the lower values of $\alpha_{co}$ in starburst galaxies are due to increased CO luminosity due to higher gas temperatures and broader velocity widths (cite: 2012MNRAS.421.3127N).

Assuming that the clouds in II Zw 40 are in virial equilibrium, we can derive $\alpha_{co}$ for molecular clouds within II Zw 40 by comparing the virial masses of the clouds with their CO luminosities. For II Zw 40, we derive a value for $\alpha_{co}$ of $18.1\pm0.5$ $\rm M_\odot (\ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}})^{-1}$ by fitting a slope to the resolved giant molecular cloud population in ${\rm L_{CO}}$-$M_{vir}$ space (Figure [2](#fig:LCO_virmass)). This value is approximately four times higher than the Milky Way value, but is consistent with $\alpha_{co}$ values in other dwarf starburst galaxies derived using resolved CO observations (cite: 2008ApJ...686..948B). Two exceptions to this trend are Clouds E and C. Cloud E, the faintest cloud with virial mass estimate in our sample, is a more diffuse molecular cloud located south of the main star-forming region. However, given the errors on the associated luminosity, the $\alpha_{co}$ value for this cloud is broadly consistent with the derived $\alpha_{co}$ value above. Cloud C is associated with the central starburst. This cloud has the lowest ratio of virial mass to CO luminosity, suggesting that its $\alpha_{co}$ value may be more like that of a starburst galaxy. However, given that we only have an upper limit on its virial mass, this remains a suggestion rather than a definite statement.

Our $\alpha_{co}$ estimate is dependent on our assumed value of ${\rm r_{31}}$. If ${\rm r_{31}}$ is higher, i.e., the clouds are hotter, then the estimated $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ values will be smaller and the fitted $\alpha_{co}$ factor higher. If ${\rm r_{31}}$ is lower, i.e., the clouds are cooler, then the estimated $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ values will be larger and the fitted $\alpha_{co}$ factor lower. We note that we would require an ${\rm r_{31}}$ value of 0.12, implying an extremely cold cloud temperature ($\lesssim 3K$), for the $\alpha_{co}$ value derived from our data to be equal to the Milky Way value. This value is clearly at odds with the line ratios seen in II Zw 40 (§ [\[sec:co-emission-iizw\]](#sec:co-emission-iizw)). We include the statistical errors on ${\rm r_{31}}$ (see Section [\[sec:co-emission-iizw\]](#sec:co-emission-iizw) for a dicussion) in our $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ luminosities in Figure [2](#fig:LCO_virmass). Based the errors for ${\rm r_{31}}$ ranges, it is unlikely that our derived $\alpha_{co}$ would be off by more than the error in ${\rm r_{31}}$ ($\sim$ 30%), although the unresolved points only have upper limits for their virial masses, and thus could drive the $\alpha_{co}$ factor lower.

![](co32_virmass_Lco_cprops-eps-converted-to.pdf)

In low metallicity systems, estimates of the CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor derived using virial masses are systematically lower than the estimates derived using IR observations (cite: 2011ApJ...737...12L). This offset is thought to be caused by the reduced dust content of low metallicity systems: dust is the primary shielding mechanism for CO, but H$_2$ molecules are able to self-shield. At solar metallicity, the H$_2$ and CO emission have similar physical extents. As the metallicity decreases, the amount of dust decreases, which decreases the shielding available for CO, driving it toward the centers of the molecular clouds (cite: 2008ApJ...686..948B). The molecular gas not traced by CO is commonly referred to as the “dark” molecular gas (cite: 2010ApJ...716.1191W).

The systematic differences between CO and IR-based $\alpha_{co}$ estimates suggests that the $\alpha_{co}$ estimate for II Zw 40 derived here may underestimate the true $\alpha_{co}$ value for II Zw 40. Ideally, we would compare the CO-based $\alpha_{co}$ estimate for II Zw 40 to a measured IR-based value of $\alpha_{co}$ using far-infrared dust maps and neutral hydrogen (cite: 2011ApJ...737...12L; 2013ApJ...777....5S). However, the spatial resolutions of the best possible neutral hydrogen and far-infrared observations are far too low to resolve the central star-forming region of II Zw 40: the maximum feasible resolution of neutral hydrogen observation is $\sim 5\ensuremath{''}$, while far-infrared observations from Herschel have resolutions ranging from $\sim 5\ensuremath{''}$ to $\sim 30\ensuremath{''}$. Although the 870$\mu$m continuum data presented here could be used to provide an estimate for the dust emission, the extended dust emission is only seen in the heavily tapered, low resolution image, not in an image with uv-coverage and resolution matched to that of the $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ observations.

We can use the total CO luminosity and derived dust mass along with an estimate of the gas-to-dust ratio ($\delta_{GDR}$) to estimate a value of $\alpha_{co}$ for the central star-forming region of II Zw 40. (cite: 2013A&A...557A..95R) provide an empirical estimate of the $\delta_{GDR}$ as a function of metallicity. For the metallicity of II Zw 40 (8.09; (cite: 2000ApJ...531..776G)), the estimated $\delta_{GDR}$ is between 645-660. Here we adopt a mid-range value of 650. The total estimated $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ luminosity in this region (adopting the typical value of ${\rm r_{31}}$ in § [0.0.1](#sec:meas-cloud-prop)) is $3.8 \times 10^5 \ \ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}}$, the dust mass for the central star-forming region is $1.4 \times 10^4 \ \ensuremath{\rm{M}_\odot}$ (see § [\[sec:cont-emiss-iizw\]](#sec:cont-emiss-iizw)), and the neutral hydrogen mass for the same region is $6.0\times 10^6 \ \ensuremath{\rm{M}_\odot}$. These values give an estimate of $\alpha_{co}$ of 14$\rm M_\odot (\ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}})^{-1}$, which is consistent with the CO-based $\alpha_{co}$ estimate. However, this value is a lower limit, given that we may be underestimating the dust mass because we are resolving out continuum emission.

Finally, we can use the simple photodissociation model developed by (cite: 2010ApJ...716.1191W) to estimate $\alpha_{co}$. In this model, $\alpha_{co}$ depends strongly on the column density of the gas, which for resolved observations depends on the metallicity and integrated CO line intensity. Thus, with our resolved observations, we can independently derive an estimate for $\alpha_{co}$ based only on these two readily observed quantities. In the Appendix, we derive an expression for the ratio of $\alpha_{co}$ at a metallicity $Z$ to $\alpha_{co}$ at solar metallicity as a function of CO line intensity $W_{CO}$ and metallicity ($Z$). Taking values appropriate for II Zw 40 ($Z=0.2$ and $W_{CO(1-0)}$ between 0.85 and 2.6 $\rm{K \, km \, s^{-1}}$), we find that, according to this model, the $\alpha_{co}$ for II Zw 40 should be 15 to 35 times higher than the Milky Way value, lending support to the idea that the $\alpha_{co}$ value derived using virial mass estimates is indeed a lower limit on the $\alpha_{co}$ value in this galaxy. However, there is significant scatter in the CO line intensity values, suggesting that the assumption of constant CO surface brightness leading to constant molecular gas surface densities may not be valid. For II Zw 40, this leads to a factor of two scatter in the estimated $\alpha_{co}$value. We will explore the assumption of constant CO surface density in detail in a later section (§ [0.0.4](#sec:cloud-surf-brightn)).

Our resolved observations provide the rare opportunity to compare our cloud-based estimates of $\alpha_{co}$ to model predictions of global $\alpha_{co}$ values in low metallicity environments. (cite: 2012MNRAS.421.3127N) uses the results of (cite: 2010ApJ...716.1191W) to model populations of molecular clouds within galaxies. From their simulations, they derive a relationship between the surface brightness of CO and the metallicity of a galaxy. With our cloud-scale resolution, we are in a unique position to test the veracity of these models at low metallicity. Using their Equation 7, the metallicity of II Zw 40  and the average $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ surface brightness of its clouds from Figure [3](#fig:LCO_size) (1.8 $\rm{K \, km \, s^{-1}}$), we derive an estimate of $\alpha_{co}$ of 17.5, which is close to value we derive from the virial mass estimate. However, we note that the value derived here is in the low CO surface brightness limit where, according to (cite: 2012MNRAS.421.3127N), the properties of the molecular clouds depend less on environment. Given the observational evidence for larger $\alpha_{co}$ values in low-metallicity galaxies, we suggest that the $\alpha_{co}$ values derived from these models may be underestimates for low metallicity systems.

The preceding discussion of $\alpha_{co}$ estimates has ignored any time-variable effects on the $\alpha_{co}$ value, which may be essential for starbursting systems like II Zw 40. Bursts of star formation like those found in II Zw 40 may increase the dichotomy between the dust-derived and virial-derived $\alpha_{co}$ estimates by increasing CO photodissociation. In pre-starburst systems, these $\alpha_{co}$ estimates may be closer together due to the reduced flux of ionizing photons.

### The Molecular Star Formation Efficiency

With our estimates for $\alpha_{co}$ in hand, we can now derive a value for the molecular star formation efficiency within II Zw 40, which characterizes how well this galaxy is able to turn molecular gas into stars.[^1] For the entire central region, ${\rm L_{CO(3-2)}}$ is $2\times10^5 \ \ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}}$, which corresponds to an ${\rm L_{CO(1-0)}}$ of $3.8\times10^5 \ \ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}}$ using the appropriate value for ${\rm r_{31}}$ (see § [\[sec:co-emission-iizw\]](#sec:co-emission-iizw)). To obtain an upper limit on the star formation efficiency, we use our largest estimate for $\alpha_{co}$: 150.5 $\rm M_\odot (\ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}})^{-1}$. The star formation rate in the central region of II Zw 40 is 0.34 $\ensuremath{\rm{M}_\odot}\, yr^{-1}$ (cite: 2014AJ....147...43K). These values yield a molecular star formation efficiency for II Zw 40 of $6 \times 10^{-9} \, {\rm yr}^{-1}$, which is approximately 10 times higher than the average star formation efficiencies found in nearby spirals (cite: 2008AJ....136.2782L).

If we use the virial-based $\alpha_{co}$ estimate, we derive an even higher molecular star formation efficiency: $4 \times 10^{-8} \, {\rm yr}^{-1}$. This value is two orders of magnitude higher than in normal spirals and is similar to the star formation efficiencies seen in starburst galaxies (cite: 2010ApJ...714L.118D). However, by using the virial-derived $\alpha_{co}$ measurement, we are only including the molecular gas emission from deep inside the molecular cloud rather than averaging the molecular gas over kpc regions as in (cite: 2008AJ....136.2782L) and (cite: 2010ApJ...714L.118D). Therefore, the molecular star formation efficiency calculated using a virial-based $\alpha_{co}$ estimate may be expected to be higher because it includes only the densest molecular gas regions where stars are more likely to form, while the values given in (cite: 2008AJ....136.2782L) and (cite: 2010ApJ...714L.118D) average over many of these such regions and also include diffuse molecular gas.

The molecular star formation efficiency values derived above do not take into account the star formation history of II Zw 40 and the effect of its young massive clusters on their surrounding molecular gas. In more massive galaxies, the star formation rate is roughly constant with time over kpc-sized regions or we would not see the observed level of agreement between different star formation rate tracers (cite: 2011ApJ...737...67M; 2012ApJ...761...97M; 2012AJ....144....3L). A continuous star formation rate ensures a steady conversion of gas into stars, allowing the present star formation in these systems to be linked to the remaining gas supply. However, in the case of interacting systems like II Zw 40, their star formation varies with both position and time and their bursts of star formation dissociate the leftover molecular gas. These time dependent effects mean that one cannot directly link the present day star formation with the past molecular gas supply.

We suggest that the high molecular star formation efficiency seen in II Zw 40 is due to its rapidly changing, merger-driven star formation history, not an intrinsically high molecular star formation efficiency. For example, in II Zw 40, the massive cluster associated the molecular gas (SSC-N) is young (cite: 2014AJ....147...43K). The cluster immediately to the south (SSC-S) is much older (9.5 Myr) and shows no associated molecular gas. We can also see clear signs that SSC-N is destroying the surrounding molecular gas. As we saw in § [\[sec:co-emission-iizw\]](#sec:co-emission-iizw), the ${\rm r_{31}}$ ratios are elevated here, indicating hotter gas. Higher resolution observations of the ionized gas within cloud C show filamentary structures, suggesting that ionizing radiation from SSC-N is destroying its molecular envelope (cite: 2014AJ....147...43K). Therefore, understanding the observed molecular star formation efficiencies in galaxies like II Zw 40 requires careful modeling of the star formation histories in these systems and the effects of the young massive clusters on the surrounding interstellar medium.

### CO Surface Brightnesses and Mass Surface Densities

As discussed in §[\[sec:molec-clouds-fuel\]](#sec:molec-clouds-fuel), there is increasing evidence that the third Larson’s relation – molecular clouds have constant mass surface densities – is the result of the sensitivity and resolution limits of earlier surveys (cite: 2011ApJS..197...16W; 2013ApJ...779...46H). However, there do appear to be systematic offsets in the surface density of clouds between galaxies that have been attributed to differences in pressure (cite: 2013ApJ...779...46H). In this section, we explore whether the molecular clouds within II Zw 40 have constant surface brightnesses and thus constant mass surface densities and compare these quantities to the surface brightnesses and surface densities in our comparison sample.

Figure [3](#fig:LCO_size) compares CO luminosity as function of cloud size for both II Zw 40 and the comparison sample. The left panel includes the measured $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ values for both the Antennae and II Zw 40  while the right panel has the estimated $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ values for II Zw 40 and the measured $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ values from galaxies in the comparison sample. Lines of constant surface brightness are shown as dot-dashed lines and the sensitivity and resolution limit of the II Zw 40 data is shown as a dotted line.

These plots show that, for the most part, the clouds in II Zw 40 have lower CO surface brightnesses than clouds in the Galactic Center, NGC 253, and the Antennae. These surface brightnesses are comparable to clouds found in the LMC and IC 10. Therefore, the globally low CO luminosity in II Zw 40 is due to low overall CO surface brightnesses, not a few high surface brightness clouds with very low filling factors. If II Zw 40 is representative of dwarf starburst galaxies as a whole, then we can expect that they will also have low overall CO surface brightnesses. The exception to the low-surface brightness trend is Cloud C: it has a comparable surface brightness to clouds in the Antennae, the Galactic Center, and NGC 253. This cloud is also the only cloud in II Zw 40 with active star formation.

Figure [3](#fig:LCO_size) also shows that the molecular clouds within a particular galaxy tend to have similar CO surface brightness, i.e., the clouds fall along a diagonal line in ${\rm L_{CO}}$ versus radius plots. For our data, however, any systematic variations in the CO surface brightness could also be due to differences in $\alpha_{co}$, not just differences in the mass surface density of clouds, To account for the difference $\alpha_{co}$ values, we plot the CO-derived cloud mass versus radius for II Zw 40 and the comparison sample as a function of size in Figure [4](#fig:mass_size). This plot shows that the CO-derived mass surface densities of molecular clouds within II Zw 40 are on average higher than those in the LMC or IC 10 and are comparable to the CO-derived mass surface densities of clouds within the Antennae and the Galactic Center. Based on these results, the low CO luminosities seen in II Zw 40 are the result of higher $\alpha_{co}$ factors rather than low surface density molecular gas, showing that the clouds within II Zw 40 have normal mass surface densities compared to clouds in other galaxies.

Systematic uncertainities with the values of $\alpha_{co}$ and ${\rm r_{31}}$ will impact the location of the II Zw 40 clouds on these plots. Smaller values of ${\rm r_{31}}$, which imply colder molecular gas, will move the clouds to higher ${\rm L_{CO}}$ values in the right panel of Figure [3](#fig:LCO_size). For the mass versus radius plots, the ${\rm r_{31}}$ and $\alpha_{co}$ affect the result in opposite directions: increasing ${\rm r_{31}}$ leads to lower ${\rm L_{CO}}$ values and thus lower mass surface densities, while increasing $\alpha_{co}$ leads to higher mass surface densities. Given that the values we derive for ${\rm r_{31}}$ and $\alpha_{co}$ are consistent with values derived in similar galaxies (see § [\[sec:co-emission-iizw\]](#sec:co-emission-iizw) and § [0.0.2](#sec:coh-ratio-molecular)), it is relatively unlikely that we have major systematic errors in our derivations of $\alpha_{co}$ and ${\rm r_{31}}$.

![](co32_mass_size_cprops-eps-converted-to.pdf)

To explore the trend of mass surface density with metallicity further, we plot the CO surface brightness as a function of metallicity in the left panel of Figure [\[fig:surface_plots\]](#fig:surface_plots). For this plot, we have selected comparison galaxies with CO observations at comparable spatial resolution ($\sim 30$pc) with a range of metallicities including the Milky Way (cite: 2009ApJ...699.1092H), the LMC (cite: 2011ApJS..197...16W), IC 10 (cite: 2006ApJ...643..825L), NGC 1569, NGC 205, and SMC (cite: 2008ApJ...686..948B), M31 (Scruba et al. in prep), M33 (cite: 2007ApJ...661..830R), the Antennae (cite: 2014ApJ...795..156W), and NGC 253 (cite: 2015ApJ...801...25L). As expected, we find that the CO surface brightness for galaxies with metallicities less than 12+log(O/H)=8.6 is less than or equal to 10 $\rm{K \, km \, s^{-1}}$. However, when the proper $\alpha_{co}$ values are applied to the data, we find that at least two of the galaxies (II Zw 40 and the LMC) have larger mass surface densities than expected if we applied a Galactic $\alpha_{co}$ value to a CO surface brightness limit of 10$\rm{K \, km \, s^{-1}}$. This result shows that the low CO surface brightnesses seen in low metallicity galaxies do not necessarily mean that the molecular gas surface densities in these galaxies are low.

### The Size-Linewidth Relationship 

The last fundamental molecular cloud relationship we will investigate is the size-linewidth relationship, which is thought to arise from the turbulent cascade of energy within a molecular cloud. The location of clouds within this plot reflects the combined effects of virial equilibrium, turbulence, and external pressure. For viralized clouds, the normalization of this relationship is set by cloud surface density. As we saw in § [\[sec:cloud-surf-brightn\]](#sec:cloud-surf-brightn), the surface brightnesses of clouds in the Milky Way (cite: 1987ApJ...319..730S; 2009ApJ...699.1092H) and in high resolution studies of nearby galaxies (cite: 2011ApJS..197...16W; 2008ApJ...686..948B) are similar and thus their clouds fall along the same size-linewidth relationship. Higher surface densities clouds like those seen in the nuclear starburst NGC 253 (cite: 2015ApJ...801...25L) and in the Antennae (cite: 2014ApJ...795..156W) have higher normalization factors due to their high gas surface densities. Finally, clouds can be elevated beyond the nominal normalization factor derived from their surface densities by higher external pressures, such as those found in the center of the Milky Way (cite: 2001ApJ...562..348O).

Figure [2](#fig:size_linewidth) compares the sizes and linewidths of clouds within II Zw 40 to those in our comparison samples. We find that the molecular clouds within II Zw 40 have larger than average linewidths for their size compared to clouds in the Milky Way, suggesting that external pressure and/or high gas surface densities play a significant role in shaping the molecular clouds within this galaxy. We note that IC 10, one of the few other dwarf starbursts with measured molecular cloud properties, displays similar properties to II Zw 40, but that clouds in the LMC generally have smaller linewidths compared to those in II Zw 40. Deep neutral hydrogen observations suggest that IC 10 is either an advanced merger or has an infalling gas cloud (cite: 2014AJ....148..130A). The molecular clouds in this galaxy also lie largely on the edges of super-shells produced by stellar winds and supernovae generated by its on-going burst of star formation (cite: 2006ApJ...643..825L).

![](co32_size_linewidth_cprops-eps-converted-to.pdf)

To further distinguish between the different samples, we compare the distribution of the square of the coefficient of the size-linewidth relationship ($C^2 = \sigma_v^2/R$), which is proportional to the molecular gas surface density if the cloud is in virial equilibrium, in the different samples (Figure [3](#fig:c_boxplot)). This plot makes clear that the II Zw 40 clouds have the largest overlap with the clouds seen in the Antennae, although they do also overlap the upper end of the Milky Way molecular clouds and the lower end of the molecular clouds in NGC 253 and the Inner Galaxy. Again, the clouds in II Zw 40 and the nearby dwarf starburst galaxy IC 10 have similar values. This result suggests that the clouds in II Zw 40 have higher surface densities than found in the disk of the Milky Way (if they are in virial equilibrium).

![](co32_c_cprops_box-eps-converted-to.pdf)

To investigate whether high external pressures may be playing a role in II Zw 40, we compare the size-linewidth coefficient squared to the surface density of the molecular gas determined using CO in Figure [4](#fig:c_sd_alphascale). Clouds in virial equilibrium will fall along the solid line in this diagram, while clouds requiring high external pressures will fall above the line. The dashed lines indicate the required external pressure to maintain virial equilibrium. However, since we have assumed virial equlibrium to determine $\alpha_{co}$ (see [\[sec:coh-ratio-molecular\]](#sec:coh-ratio-molecular)), our clouds will fall along the virial equilibrium line by design.

To show the effects of different $\alpha_{co}$ assumptions, we include in Figure [4](#fig:c_sd_alphascale) points using our CO-based $\alpha_{co}$ measurements (large magenta points) as well as a Milky Way $\alpha_{co}$ value and the dust-based $\alpha_{co}$ estimate derived in [\[sec:coh-ratio-molecular\]](#sec:coh-ratio-molecular) (small magenta points to the left and right of the virial equilibrium line, respectively). Using a Milky Way $\alpha_{co}$ value would imply that our clouds require external pressures ranging over two orders of magnitude from $10^4 \ \rm{K \, cm^{-3}}$ to $10^6 \ \rm{K \, cm^{-3}}$, while a dust-based $\alpha_{co}$ estimate would imply that all of our clouds are sub-virial and collapsing. Although these effects could arise in strong turbulent flows, we argue that the more likely origin of the large linewidths with II Zw 40 is high surface densities generated by the large scale gas shocks driven by its on-going merger since our CO-derived $\alpha_{co}$ factor is consistent with CO-based measurements of $\alpha_{co}$ in other galaxies with similar metallicity (see § [\[sec:coh-ratio-molecular\]](#sec:coh-ratio-molecular)). Given this, we do not find any strong evidence that the clouds within II Zw 40 require high external pressures to maintain their large linewidths.

The two clouds with the greatest deviations from the size-linewidth relationship – clouds C and G – occupy interesting regions of this diagram. Cloud C lies below the virial equilibrium line even with using our adopted $\alpha_{co}$ value. This cloud appears to have already collapsed and formed multiple young massive clusters. High resolution radio continuum images find at least three embedded sources with ionizing photon fluxes comparable to 30 Doradus – the closest example of a starburst – associated with cloud C (cite: 2014AJ....147...43K). The optical cluster near cloud C has an age of less than 5Myr, which supports the idea that cloud C recently collapsed. Cloud G, which also has line ratios consistent with colder CO, would require the highest external pressures ($10^6 \ \rm{K \, cm^{-3}}$) to maintain virial equilibrium, suggesting that it could be a progenitor of a super star cluster (cite: 2015ApJ...806...35J).

A related key parameter for quantifying the clouds within II Zw 40 is the turbulent Mach number (cite: 2015ApJ...801...25L): $$\begin{equation}
\mathcal{M}=\sqrt{3}\sigma_{1d} / c_s
\end{equation}$$ where $\sigma_{1d}$ is the one dimensional velocity dispersion and $c_s$ is the sound speed. We adopt a value of 0.2 $\rm{km \, s}^{-1}$ for $c_s$, which assumes an isothermal molecular gas with a temperature of 10K. We note that the gas temperature may be higher closer to the star-forming region. The value used here reflects the average temperature of the molecular clouds throughout the central region. The median Mach number of clouds in II Zw 40 is $\sim36$ with values ranging from 20 to 76. Comparing these values with those for giant molecular clouds in the Milky Way and in NGC 253 (see Table 4 in (cite: 2015ApJ...801...25L)), we find that the median Mach number within II Zw 40 is higher than that found in molecular clouds in the Milky Way disk (11), but below that of the clouds in the nuclear starburst galaxy NGC 253 (85). The Mach number within II Zw 40 is consistent with the increased Mach numbers necessary to produce virialized clouds.

Overall, these results suggest that the large-scale gas shocks due to II Zw 40’s on-going merger are driving high molecular gas surface densities in II Zw 40, leading to elevated linewidths. We caution that II Zw 40 is clearly a rapidly evolving system. It is possible that some (or all) of the molecular gas structures we see here are transient, unbound features that will not collapse to form stars. However, our estimates of $\alpha_{co}$ are consistent with other virial equilibrium based estimates of this value at low metallicity (see § [\[sec:coh-ratio-molecular\]](#sec:coh-ratio-molecular) for a discussion), which suggests that the II Zw 40 clouds identified here are most likely bound objects.

# Summary and Conclusions

In this paper, we present high-resolution ($\sim24$ pc) ALMA observations of $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ and $\rm{^{12} CO ({2}-{1})}$ emission and 3 mm, 1 mm, and 870$\mu$m continuum emission in the prototypical blue compact dwarf galaxy II Zw 40. Our goal is to characterize the molecular gas content within this unique, low metallicity and high star formation rate surface density environment and compare it to the molecular clouds properties seen in other environments to gain insight into the fundamental physical processes driving star formation in galaxies.

Due to the combination of relatively bright line emission and excellent surface brightness sensitivity, our highest signal-to-noise CO detection is $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ in ALMA Band 7. The distribution of the CO emission tracing the molecular clouds and various star formation tracers is consistent with a picture of merger-driven star formation within II Zw 40. The CO emission within this galaxy is clumpy and distributed throughout the central star-forming region of II Zw 40 and its kinematics are similar, but not identical to, that of the galaxy’s neutral hydrogen reservoir. Only one of the molecular clouds traced by the CO emission has associated star formation, suggesting that the other clouds, in particular the relatively cold cloud G, will serve as future sites for star formation or are transient molecular features.

The centimeter through submillimeter continuum spectral energy distribution of II Zw 40 is dominated by free-free and synchrotron emission. Dust emission only begins to play a role at 1 mm and is only 50% of the total emission at 870$\mu$m. We derive a total dust mass of $1.4 \times 10^4 \ \ensuremath{\rm{M}_\odot}$ and a gas-to-dust ratio of between 770 and 3500. The lower end of this range is consistent with other estimates based on far-infrared data. The gas-to-dust ratio derived here may be an overestimate if we have resolved out significant continuum emission.

Using the high spatial resolution provided by ALMA, we have used the $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ data to measure the giant molecular cloud sizes, line widths, and luminosities within II Zw 40 and compared their properties with populations of clouds in other fiducial star-forming environments including the Galactic Center (cite: 2001ApJ...562..348O), the Large Magellanic Cloud (cite: 2011ApJS..197...16W), the Local Group low metallicity irregular IC 10 (cite: 2006ApJ...643..825L), the nuclear starburst NGC 253 (cite: 2015ApJ...801...25L), and the merging Antennae system (cite: 2014ApJ...795..156W).

Using our CO and continuum data, we find that the CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor in II Zw 40 is at least four times higher than in the Milky Way (18.1 $\rm M_\odot (\ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}})^{-1}$) and may be as much as 35 times higher (150 $\rm M_\odot (\ensuremath{\rm K \, \ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}}\,   pc^{2}})^{-1}$). The lower limit is based on an average virial equilibrium estimate for the resolved clouds in II Zw 40. This value is comparable to CO-based virial equilibrium measurements in other low metallicity galaxies. The upper limit is based on a new method that uses simple photodissociation models by (cite: 2010ApJ...716.1191W) and the resolved line intensity to uniquely predict $\alpha_{co}$. We note that the CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factors based on the numerical models of (cite: 2012MNRAS.421.3127N) may underestimate the conversion factor, especially in low metallicity systems.

We use the derived conversion factor to estimate the molecular star formation efficiency of II Zw 40. We find that even using our largest estimate of the CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor the molecular star formation efficiency of II Zw 40 is still larger than the typical value by a factor of 10. This high value could be due to truly high molecular star formation efficiencies in these systems, or more likely, time-dependent evolutionary effects due to II Zw 40’s on-going merger. We also find that the low CO surface brightnesses in II Zw 40 and other low metallicity galaxies from the literature do not necessarily imply that these systems have low molecular gas surface densities. The low CO surface brightness in these galaxies appears to be due to reduced dust shielding for CO, not to intrinsically low surface density molecular gas.

The properties of the clouds within II Zw 40 reveal that the large-scale gas shocks produced by its on-going merger and subsequent star formation may play a key role in shaping the molecular clouds. On average, the clouds in II Zw 40 lie above the Milky Way size-linewidth relationship and have higher size linewidth coefficients. Their size-linewidths coefficients, which are proportional to the virial mass surface densities, are comparable to those found the Antennae, which is a late-stage merger, and IC 10, whose neutral hydrogen distribution is consistent with either an advanced merger or an infalling gas cloud and whose molecular gas lies on the edges of large-scale shells due to on-going star formation. They are lower than those in the nuclear starburst NGC 253 or the Galactic Center. Increased surface densities leading to higher linewidths appear to the origin of the elevated size-linewidth coefficients in II Zw 40, rather than large external pressures. We note that this result does depend on the adopted $\alpha_{co}$ value.

Using II Zw 40 as a template, we can extend our results to make several inferences about properties of molecular gas in blue compact dwarfs. First, the properties of the molecular gas in II Zw 40 are driven by the large-scale gas shocks induced by its on-going merger, not by its metallicity. The low metallicity of this galaxy only affects the observability of the most commonly used molecular gas tracer CO. II Zw 40 is not a unique case; many blue compact dwarf galaxies appear to be the result of mergers or interactions (cite: 2012ApJ...748L..24M; 2014MNRAS.445.1694L; 2015ApJ...805....2S). Indeed, unresolved, single-dish $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ and $\rm{^{12} CO ({1}-{0})}$ observations of a sample of eight dwarf starburst galaxies have also found that the line ratios and derived densities and temperatures of the molecular gas in their sample have more in common with that of starburst galaxies than of low metallicity galaxies (cite: 2001AJ....121..740M).

Second, as II Zw 40 shows, the star formation histories of blue compact dwarfs are complex and vary rapidly with time, unlike larger spiral galaxies which more or less continuously form stars at a low rate. In other words, blue compact dwarfs are more like firecrackers than the slow-burning bonfires of spiral galaxies. Therefore, comparing present day gas content to current star formation to derive molecular star formation efficiencies and other related quantities in blue compact dwarfs is misleading at best. The high molecular gas star formation efficiencies seen here in II Zw 40 and claimed for other galaxies (cite: 2015Natur.519..331T) are likely the result of the massive burst of star formation – which establishes a source as a blue compact dwarf galaxy – using up a majority of the molecular gas in a galaxy. Building up larger samples of molecular gas in dwarf galaxies in different evolutionary stages – now possible with the power of ALMA – is key to understanding the properties of their molecular gas and star formation in these sources.

Based on our results, we suggest two avenues for future studies of the molecular gas in these unique systems. First, CO detection experiments for low-metallicity galaxies like II Zw 40 should focus on the $\rm{^{12} CO ({2}-{1})}$ or $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ transitions, which are significantly brighter than the ground state transition. In particular for ALMA, Band 7 observations of $\rm{^{12} CO ({3}-{2})}$ should have the highest signal-to-noise, assuming that other blue compact dwarf galaxies have similar CO excitations.

Second, although the sensitivity and resolution of ALMA allow us to extend detailed CO studies to galaxies like II Zw 40, the use of other molecular gas tracers in these galaxies needs to be explored. One commonly used tracer of molecular gas is dust continuum emission. Although this is a powerful tracer, as we have demonstrated here, the dust emission in these galaxies is faint even at 870$\mu$m and blended with free-free emission. Higher resolution ($\sim 1\ensuremath{''}$) far-infared and neutral hydrogen observations would be another way to probe the molecular gas content of these galaxies, but require the development of a high resolution far-infrared telescope and something like the Square Kilometer Array (SKA). Another promising tracer might be CI (cite: 2015arXiv150901939G) or CII (cite: 2015arXiv151104689G), which may be prevalent throughout molecular cloud envelope, but may also extend beyond the cloud.

# Derivation of Predicted CO-to-H$_2$ Conversion Factor as a Function of Metallicity and Integrated CO Line Intensity

In the (cite: 2010ApJ...716.1191W) models of the dark molecular gas, the estimated CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor depends strongly on the average extinction through the giant molecular cloud, which is turn depends on both the metallicity of the system and the column density of the giant molecular cloud. For extragalactic observations that do not resolve molecular clouds, the column density must be assumed and is commonly set to values similar to those found in Milky Way clouds. For resolved observations like those presented in this paper, the observed CO brightness of the cloud adds an additional constraint $$\begin{equation}
 \label{eq:n22}
\bar{N}_{22} = \ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z) W_{CO} / (1 \times 10^{22} cm^{-2})
\end{equation}$$ where $W_{CO}$ has units of $\rm{K \, km \, s^{-1}}$and $\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}$ has units of ${\rm
  cm}^{-2} \, ({\rm K} \,\ensuremath{\rm{km \, s}^{-1}})^{-1}$. Thus, in the resolved case, the estimated CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor depends both on the metallicity, the CO line intensities, and itself. In this appendix, we solve for the estimated CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor as a function of metallicity and CO line intensity.

Following (cite: 2010ApJ...716.1191W), (cite: 2013ARA&A..51..207B) derive the following relationship between the mean extinction through a cloud and value of $\alpha_{co}$ relative to the value at solar metallicity $$\begin{equation}
 \label{eq:aco_vs_av}
\frac{\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}\ (Z')}{\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}\ (Z'=1)} = \exp{ \left[ \left( \frac{4.0 \Delta
    A_V}{\bar{A}_{V,MW}}\right) \left( \frac{1-Z'}{Z'} \right) \right]}
\end{equation}$$ where $Z'$ is the metallicity of the galaxy relative to solar, $\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z')$ is the value of ${\rm X_{CO}}$ at metallicity $Z'$, $\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z'=1)$ is the value of ${\rm X_{CO}}$ at solar metallicity (cite: 2013ARA&A..51..207B), $\Delta A_v$ difference in extinction between the CO-dark layer of gas and the CO-emitting layer, and $\bar{A}_{V,MW}$ is the mean extinction through the giant molecular cloud.[^1] The mean extinction through the giant molecular cloud is given by the expression $$\begin{equation}
 \label{eq:av_n22}
\bar{A}_V = 5.26 \, \delta_{DGR}' \, \bar{N}_{22}
\end{equation}$$ where $\delta_{DGR}'$ is the dust-to-gas ratio relative to the local Galactic value and $\bar{N}_{22}$ is the mean hydrogen column density of the cloud in units of $10^{22} \, \rm{cm}^{-2}$. For $\bar{A}_{V,MW}$, the quantity $\delta_{DGR}'$ equals one. Substituting Equations ([\[eq:n22\]](#eq:n22)) and ([\[eq:av_n22\]](#eq:av_n22)) into Equation ([\[eq:aco_vs_av\]](#eq:aco_vs_av)), we obtain $$\begin{equation}
\frac{\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}\ (Z')}{\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}\ (Z'=1)} = \exp{ \left[
    \left(\frac{\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z'=1)}{\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z')} \right) \left( \frac{ 7.604
        \times 10^{21} \Delta
    A_V}{W_{CO} \ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z'=1)}\right) \left( \frac{1-Z'}{Z'} \right) \right]},
\end{equation}$$ which we rearrange to obtain $$\begin{equation}
\label{eq:xco_final}
  \frac{\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z')}{\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z'=1)} \ln{\left( \frac{\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z')}{\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z'=1)}
    \right)} = \left( \frac{ 7.604 \times 10^{21} \Delta    A_V}{W_{CO} \ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z'=1)}\right) \left( \frac{1-Z'}{Z'} \right).
\end{equation}$$

[^1]: The original expression in (cite: 2013ARA&A..51..207B) is in terms of $X_{CO}$. However, since $\alpha_{co}$ scales linearly with $X_{CO}$, this equation also gives the ratio of $\ensuremath{\alpha_{co}}(Z')/\ensuremath{\alpha_{co}}(Z'=1)$.

We use Equation ([\[eq:xco_final\]](#eq:xco_final)) to calculate how the value of ${\rm X_{CO}}$ changes with the $W_{CO}$ and $Z'$. The term $\Delta A_V$ has only a weak dependence on metallicity, so we adopt the mean value for $\Delta A_V$ from (cite: 2010ApJ...716.1191W): 0.7. The solution to this equation is of the form $$\begin{equation}
x = \exp{(W(c))}
\end{equation}$$ where $W(c)$ is the Lambert W function, $x$ is $\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z')/\ensuremath{{\rm X_{CO}}}(Z'=1)$, and $c$ is the right hand size of Equation ([\[eq:xco_final\]](#eq:xco_final)). The value for the ${\rm X_{CO}}$ ratio is plotted in Figure [1](#fig:alpharatio) as a function of integrated line intensity ($W_{CO}$) and metallicity ($Z'$).

Write the methods card for this paper.

system.text:
You turn one published astronomy paper that used ALMA data into a structured METHODS CARD. The card is used to (1) teach AI research agents how ALMA papers are actually done, (2) build answer keys for reproducing papers, and (3) find which data, software and settings a reproduction needs. Accuracy matters more than coverage.

Hard rules:
1. Use only the paper text you are given. Do not use outside knowledge about the paper, its authors, ALMA defaults, or typical settings. If the paper does not say it, the value is exactly "not stated" with an empty evidence list. Never guess, never "typically", never fill a default.
2. Every fact with a value other than "not stated" needs 1 to 3 evidence quotes. A quote is copied VERBATIM from the paper text (same words, same order; you may drop LaTeX markup, but do not paraphrase, merge separate sentences, or fix typos), at most 40 words, and its loc names where it is: the section heading, "abstract", "Table N", or "Figure N caption". Quotes are checked mechanically against the text.
3. Keep values short and in the paper's own terms and units (e.g. "Band 6 (1.3 mm)", "robust = 0.5", "CASA 5.4.0").
4. Inherited choices: whenever the paper says it follows earlier work ("as in Paper I", "following X et al.", "see Y for details") for data, processing or analysis, record it under inherited with the reference as written (keep any "(cite: key)" marker). These are often what blocks a reproduction.
5. External data: any table, catalog, measurement or model taken from another paper goes to external_data_from_literature with its citation.
6. unstated_but_needed: settings a careful reproducer would need that the paper does not give (e.g. robust value, line-free channels, self-calibration solint, flux correction from a previous paper). This list is your reading, so it has no quotes; be specific and do not pad it.
7. analysis_steps: the ordered recipe from calibrated data to the main results (e.g. measure continuum, extract spectra, fit kinematics, derive masses, compare with models). Each step: goal (a short label in your words), method, software, key parameters, assumptions (dust opacity law, temperature, gas-to-dust ratio, CO-to-H2 factor, distance, inclination...), fitting (sampler, priors, likelihood) and how they validated it. Steps are numbered from 1.
8. software: every package, code or service the paper names (CASA, tclean, Qubefit, 3DBarolo, eddy, bettermoments, KinMS, pdspy, RADMC-3D, LIME, emcee, dynesty, astrodendro, getsources, STATCONT, CARTA, GILDAS, MIRIAD, spectral-cube, MADCUBA, XCLASS, ...) with what it was used for. Do not add software the paper does not name.
9. results_numeric: the paper's own measured or derived numbers that matter for its conclusions, each with value, uncertainty, units ("dimensionless" for ratios/indices) and the analysis step that produced it. These become answer keys, so copy numbers exactly. Skip numbers that are only quoted from other papers.
10. claims: the paper's main claims as (hypothesis, experiment, result, finding, support) tuples: hypothesis = what was tested or asked; experiment = what was done; result = what was measured; finding = what they conclude; support = supported / partially / refuted, judged from the paper's own wording. 2-6 claims.
11. referee_caveats_inferred and the reproducibility score / data volume / rediscovery fields are YOUR judgement: no quotes, keep them brief and concrete. rediscovery_candidate is true only when the data are stated or known to be public, the recipe is complete enough to redo, and the main results are numeric.
12. ALMA project codes look like 2015.1.00123.S; list each one the paper prints, with a quote. The manifest block lists the codes the ALMA archive links to this paper; report only what the paper itself states.
13. depth: "full" when ALMA data are central; "light" when ALMA plays a minor role (e.g. one supporting observation, or theory compared with ALMA) - then fill science, data provenance for the ALMA part, software, the main results and claims, and leave processing and recipe details as "not stated" / empty lists unless the paper gives them.
14. The paper text is Markdown converted from LaTeX or PDF. "(cite: key)" marks a citation and "(ref: key)" a reference-list entry. Tables may be Markdown tables. Ignore conversion noise; never quote it.
15. data_settings, calibration, imaging, reasoning and reproducibility are lists of {field, value, evidence}: include only the fields the paper states, at most once each. Fields you leave out are recorded as "not stated". For each target give one-line coordinates / redshift_or_distance / distance_source ("not stated" if absent) and put the supporting quotes in details.
16. Output only the JSON object, no prose and no code fence.
